speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I call attention of the government to a despatch from Washington which, no doubt, all hon. members have read, to the effect that a communication has passed from this government to the United States intimating an unwillingness to complv with a request that had been made for cooperation in the prevention of shipments of liquor against the law into the United States. Would the government intimate what correspondence has been sent from Washington to this government and from this government to Washington on the subject?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am obliged to my right hon. friend for bringing up the matter, because, having read the despatches to which he refers, I think they are calculated to create an entirely erroneous impression. It is true, the government has received from Washington a communication asking if it would be possible for the Canadian government to assist in promoting the observance of certain liquor laws of the United States. The communication relates to mattens particularly appertaining to the export of liquor. When the communication was received it was referred to the departments of government concerned. The reply sent to Washington related exclusively to a statement of the law as it stands and the position of the Canadian authorities in meeting the request that has been made. There has been nothing sent forward to Washington with respect to the government's policy in the matter of endeavouring to co-operate with American authorities in securing observance of their laws. So far as' the government's policy in that matter is concerned, I would say that we have every desire to co-operate with the American authorities in helping	them to secure	the
observance of their laws in precisely the same manner as we would hope to have the American authorities co-operate with us in
securing the observance__of our laws. Such
action as has been taken up to the present has been entirely of a departmental character. The government is sending a communication to Washington intimating that, as soon as the present session is over, we will be pleased to receive at Ottawa	an	officer	from	theAmerican government	to	discuss	with	ourofficials possible ways	and	means	ot neipmg
to meet the situation to which they have referred. Our attitude in this matter is entirely a friendly one, in an endeavour to fur-

ther, so far as it may be possible for us so to do, the best of relations with our American neighbours.

When did the request
come? And, was there not time to receive the American delegate so that the government's policy might get beyond the bounds of desire and into legislation? I noted that the Prime Minister stated that they had taken care that the delegate would not come until the session was through, when it is impossible to put any more legislation on the statute books for another year. When was the request received and why was action not taken before?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The request
was received some little time ago. When it was received, it was referred to the departments of government concerned, and I think such delay as has taken place has arisen out of the circumstance that legal opinion had to be given by the law officers as to the position of the law, and the extent to which it would be possible to go under the law as it stands in meeting the situation as presented to us. My impression is that it was about three months ago, the request was received. There was no intention of delay in the matter. It was dealt with entirely departmentally. As regards the larger question, that of policy, the government would like to be able to view all sides of the situation before taking final action.

Mr. Speaker, I beg to ask leave, under rule 39, to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, to call the attention of the House to certain statements appearing in the press, apparently of an authentic nature, regarding the financial position of the Union Bank of Canada; and the necessity of safe-guarding the public interest in every possible way.

Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to move the adjournment?
And leave having been granted:

Might I remind hon.
members of rule 39, paragraph (c) which reads:
The motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session.
I merely wish to call the attention of hon. members who might desire to speak on the motion, that they must speak strictly to the the motion. fMr. Mackenzie King.]

Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to keep to the motion as closely as I possibly can, although I realize that it will, perhaps, be a little difficult to deal with this matter without in some way alluding to what has been taking place in this House and in different committees for some time past. The House has only passed the third reading of the Bank Act renewing the charters for another ten years, and now the affairs of one of our large chartered banks has been made public, and the people are made aware that the bank has suffered some losses, so that, perhaps, it is in the public interest that this question should be discussed to some extent at the present time.
A statement has been made by the president and directors of the Union Bank of Canada. I may say that for some time back there have been persistent rumours in the country that all has not been well with some of our banks. We have heard this in the corridors of the House, and I have heard it mentioned in other places. We are assured by an examination of the bank's affairs by auditors, president, directors, and an independent high official of the Bank of Montreal, that the Union Bank is in a fundamentally sound position. It seems strange, though this may be only a coincidence, that just immediately after the third reading of the Bank Act had passed this House, the statement was made public. This may have been only a coincidence, and just happened; but on the face of the matter, it seems rather strange that this should have taken place. I have no wish by word or act of mine to do anything that will in any way throw doubts or cause uneasiness in regard to the position of the Union Bank of Canada at this particular time. I want, however, to call the attention of the House to a statement issued by the Union Bank of Canada on November 30, 1922. The statement in part is as follows:
Capital	 $8,000,000
Net profits for the year after all bad debts and. doubtful liabilities to the bank
are eliminated	 1,131,060
Paid in dividends	up	to	date

I am sure everyone must have considered that to be a most reassuring statement. The bank was prosperous, everything was going well, and no one had any reason to believe, even as late as November last, that anything was wrong. We have another statement issued just the other day. The capital remains the same, 88,000,000; the rest account has now shrunk to $1,750,000, and the

The Union Bank
profit and loss account is only 8159,360. What has happened? A sum of 84,250,000 has disappeared from the rest account of the bank. We are told that this has been withdrawn from the rest account, and placed in the contingency reserve account, presumably to cover up losses that have occurred in the bank's business during those months. The business of the bank has suffered losses from high officials of the bank. The president's statement is that this was through unauthorized transactions in sterling exchange. That is the explanation we get. I isaid previously that this all becomes public after the bill renewing bank charters for ten years had passed its third reading in this House.
Another question might be asked. There have been persistent rumours, as I have already stated, and the condition spoken of must have been in existence for months. Had the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), cr the Department of Finance, any knowledge of the condition of things during the time the Bank Act was before the committee on Banking? It might be worth while to inquire how the losses have been incurred. Have they been incurred by granting loans at branch banks where loans have been made by managers of branch banks at from 8 to 10 per cent interest? We have often heard it stated that a high rate of interest has to be charged in the prairie provinces because the risks there were much greater than in other parts of the Dominion, and 8 per cent and 10 per cent have been named as the rates of interest that had to be charged in order to carry on the bank's business successfully. What is the fact? The losses that have been incurred are not made in the branches, but through loans made at the headquarters of the bank. We know that branch managers are not allowed to make any loans over $500 without applying to headquarters for authority to do so. The facts of the case seem to be that the really serious loans made by banks are made at headquarters and by the general managers. We might say that this is due to rather reckless financing on the part of some of the managers at headquarters; witness the case of the Merchants Bank and the loss at this time incurred by the Union Bank. The thought of many people may be: Have we just escaped another merger? A concentration of one or two banks in one of the financial centres would be a misfortune, something that the Progressive party has been fighting very strenuously against. The Union Bank is the only large bank with headquarters in the West. No one wants to see it disappear; no one wants the control of 274i
credit to fall into the hands of a few privileged individuals or corporations, and I believe that this is true of the majority of our people irrespective of their views on banks and banking.
Now, let us for a moment examine some of the occurrences of recent date in banking circles. We will take the case of two banks, the Merchants Bank and the Union Bank cf Canada. The Merchants Bank suffered losses through bad loans much in the same way, I think, as the Union Bank of Canada has no doubt suffered. Still its capital was intact and it had a rest account of $1,500,000. After certain negotiations, however, it capitulated shall I say?-to the Bank of Montreal in which it was swallowed up. This, of course, resulted in a loss to its shareholders, and inconvenience and hardship to many individuals. And now, there remains of that institution no more than a name,-a name, I might say, "to point a moral or adorn a tale." The Union Bank of Canada, the one more immediately under discussion, like the Merchants Bank of Canada, has its capital stock still unimpaired, with a rest account of Sl,-750,000. These are almost parallel cases you may say, and you naturally ask the question, why so different a conclusion? To the ordinary layman outside, there does not seem to be very much difference between the respective positions of the two banks, and one naturally wonders why the ending is not the same in the one case as it was in the other. Well, the Union Bank has shown courage in the situation in which it finds itself. I think it may be commended on its courageous facing of the facts and its taking the people into its confidence. It has set its house in order, having learned from experience that the policy it has adopted is the best under the circumstances.
Now, we are told in the statement made public that there is to be a policy of economy in operating and overhead expenses. I believe I heard that same statement made not very long ago when it was declared that all the banks in Canada were running at a minimum of expense. It was stated that no reduction could be made in the matter of operating and overhead expenses, the banks apparently, as one would infer, being already run as economically as possible. Yet here we find a bank to-day making the public announcement that it will inaugurate improvements in this direction. It must be perfectly evident to a great many persons, I should think, that the operating and overhead expenses of banks to-day are much too extrava-
The Union Bank

gant in the present condition in which the country is struggling. There have been some dismissals, and perhaps this is well. I want to pay a tribute to some of the directors who are still on the board of the Union Bank. Personally I am acquainted with some of these gentlemen; they are men of probity, courage and honesty, whose names, I think, ought to be a tower of strength in restoring confidence in the stability and the fundamental soundness of the Union Bank of Canada. I have no desire for a moment to cast any shadow of doubt on the soundness of this bank. True mistakes have been made, but the right course has been adopted, and the bank deserves the support and confidence of the public in view of the courage with which it has faced the situation. But what assurance have we that the same thing may not occur again? I anticipate the probable reply, that you cannot prevent men from taking chances and doing foolish things, that you cannot make men honest by any preventive measures; honest,-shall I say?-with other people's money. Well, that does not make for stability or public confidence and I claim that something ought certainly to be done to ensure the public against any disastrous happenings in connection with the banks, at least, with the authority of any directors. In the light of experience, and in view of the facts that are now made public, parliament, by extending the bank charters for ten years has given the O.K. to things just as they are. Some hon. members may be excused for thinking that it might have been the part of wisdom for this House to have thought carefully over our whole banking system in relation to commerce and agriculture, and in relation to the needs of the common people, before partly committing itself for ten years.
Taking up the newspaper to-day I saw a short report of a speech that had been delivered by President Harding during the course of a tour through the United States. I would direct the attention of the House to some remarks he made on that occasion. He said:
For the first time in the history of agriculture in any country adequate investment and working capital will be furnished farmers on terms as favourable as those accorded to commerce and industry. The farmer is receiving nothing more than is coming to him, nothing more than he needed, nothing more than was good for him, and nothing that was not also good for all our national interests.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just a word in conclusion. I do not want to cast any reflections upon any bank or banking system at this particular time, but I do not think that the mo-
ment is opportune when something should be done to meet the situation that exists in Canada to-day. We have not yet reached a solution of the banking question; it is still open; and it would have been in the best interest of every one concerned if a little more consideration could have been given to this public question in the light of some of the revelations that have come to our knowledge in the last few days. I have just read some of the remarks of President Harding, and T realize that in this House there is a very different attitude towards the trouble of agriculture from that which was evident long ago: it is true we get a good deal of sympathy. But sometimes it is thought that those who represent the agricultural interests are sectional in their outlook on things and do not take a wide enough view of conditions as they generally prevail throughout the country. Here is President Harding making the statement that in the United States agriculture is of national importance and that anything that helps the industry must be for the general welfare. How much more is this true of a country like Canada whose great basic industry is this same agriculture? I repeat, therefore, that all our banking and our commercial interests should be viewed in their relation to the interests of agriculture in this Dominion. I do not desire to detain the House any longer, but I hope that nothing will be said to-day that will be regarded as casting any doubts on the fundamental soundness of the Union Bank. Its managers have taken the proper step, but mistakes having been made in the past, I think something should be done to obviate a recurrence of them.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I am to keep within the compass of the ruling laid down by you, Mr. Speaker, as to the nature of the present discussion, I am afraid that I cannot follow my hon. friend (Mr. Forke) in the consideration of the recent address of President Harding. President Harding's notions of what is good to help agriculture do not happen always to be in harmony with our own. For example, he thinks that one way to help agriculture is to put an enormously high tariff against the Canadian west, and so I am not disposed to regard him as a high authority on matters of that sort. I am unable to see the connection, if there is any, between the Bank Act and the present affairs of the Union Bank of Canada. If all that we know about the affairs of the Union Bank had been before us from the beginning of the session, I fail to see what bearing it would have upon the amendments to the Bank

The Union Bank
Act. I would welcome, even at this eleventh hour, any useful suggestions that might be offered by way of amendment to that act; and the act, let me inform my hon. friend, is not yet absolutely through parliament. At this moment, it is before another branch of parliament, and if hon. gentlemen feel interested in any question touching the Union Bank trouble, if they will frame some reasonable amendment dealing with the matter, I am sure that even to-day hon. gentlemen of the Senate would be willing to consider it.
My hon. friend asks two questions. First, he wants to know whether the information concerning the Union Bank was in the possession of the Minister of Finance before the Bank Act passed. Yes; and under what circumstances I will tell him. He also asks the question, what assurance have we that this thing may not be repeated? I can tell him that we have no assurance, and so long as human nature is as it is we cannot have any assurance, that misfortunes may not occur to any bank. We cannot guarantee the banking skill nor the moral character of any banking officials. Do not let us run away with the idea that we can make men moral, in the matter of banking, by act of parliament. Men will always receive positions of trust, and if they betray that trust or display bad management in the execution of it, we can only regret the weakness of poor humanity. My hon. friend, however, asks a more important question: Did we know anything of this trouble of the Union Bank when the Bank Act was still before the committee? I personally knew about it, yes; and I will tell my hon. friend the circumstances. About a month ago the president of the Union Bank, Mr. Allan, sent a special messenger to me from Winnipeg. He brought a return of the last month's operations of the bank. He filed that return in accordance with the law, and the messenger, speaking for Mr. Allan, said, "While the president files this return, and while it is in accordance with the statements in the books' of the company and is correct in that respect, he feels anxious. He is not himself satisfied with the return. He finds a condition has arisen which calls for investigation. He is not prepared to make a definite statement now, but he believes the bank has suffered losses which need to be accounted for in a different manner from that indicated in the return." He was kind enough to ask my judgment and advice as to what should be done. I told him the only advice I could presume to give, although probably it was not necessary, was for him to have a thorough investigation into the affairs of the bank to ascertain the exact condition; that
if losses had been incurred, his proper course was to ascertain them as absolutely and definitely as possible, and then come before the public and make a frank statement of the whole situation. Mr. Read, the auditor, who brought the message to me, intimated that that was exactly what was in the mind of the president and directors of the bank. He told me their officials were making an inquiry into the bank's affairs and intended to call in the expert of another bank to confirm, if necessary, their judgment.
They reached a conclusion and in due course a statement was made to the public. The only communication I received at that time is the one which I shall now read. As I said, Sir, the message came to me by special messenger from Winnipeg, President Allan did not come himself but sent the auditor, Mr. Read. On June 5 I received the following letter from Mr. Allan:
Dear Sir,
As you will remember a verbal statement was made to you on my instructions by Mr. E. S. Read, the auditor of the Union Bank of Canada at the time of the filing of our April statement with your department to the effect that while the statement was correct according to the books of the bank, I had reason to fear the existence of losses the extent of which I was unaware of: that as a consequence I had instituted a revaluation of the Bank's assets, the result of which was not then known but which it was feared might necessitate the deduction of a considerable sum from the Rest Account, and that our April statement was filed in your department subject to the outcome of that revaluation. Its completion has been delayed beyond the date anticipated but I expect that within ten days or two weeks I shall be able to intimate the result to you and that our statement for May will be prepared in accordance therewith.
I am, Sir,
Yours sincerely,
W. R. Allan,
President.
Now, I have every reason to believe that the action of the president and directors of the Union Bank of Canada was' in accordance with the advice that I ventured to give them-indeed, my advice was not necessary, they had already undertaken to do this. The statement has been issued to the public and the House is familiar with it. I commend the action of the president and directors in the course they took. When they discovered there were losses- beyond those for which they had made provision, they had courage to face the music, to make an investigation, to ascertain the exact extent of the losses, to make reasonable provision for those losses by writing down their assets, and then to come before the country with a full, frank statement. In that way, I believe, they have deserved and have won the confidence of the country. I have no reason to doubt that the Union Bank is in a sound and strong position, and
Questions

again I congratulate the president and directors upon the courage they have evinced.
Beyond this I do not know that I have anything to say regarding the Union Bank of Canada. This is the whole story.

1.	If dockages are all b:nned together and terminal elevators clean that which belongs to them, how do they deliver to the purchaser the quality which they themselves (the elevators) receive?
2.	Is it possible to obtain sample from the inspection department representing quality of dockage used by inspectors when grading dockage shipped and as shown by inspector''s test as provided for in the tariff?
3.	Who determines the standards by which inspectors inspect and grade dockage for which no standard has been set by the Standards board?
4.	What provision is made for the inspection of spelts and mixed grain?
5.	In case of dispute can survey be held on spelts and mixed grain?

1.	Terminal elevators are required to deliver all screenings free from domestic grain other than broken wheat, and to deliver to the owner of said screenings what would be considered a fair average of original screenings after separation of domestic grain is made.
2.	No. It is not possible to obtain sample from the Inspection department that would represent quality of dockage, as the Inspection department do not grade dockage; but it is possible to obtain sample from the Inspection department representing quality of dockage covering any particiilar shipment after same is loaded.
3.	There are no standards set by the Standards board covering dockage. The only standard which the inspectors use is that defined by the Seed Commissioner for "Standard Re-cleaned Screenings."
4.	No provision is made for the classification of spelts, but dockage would be assessed if not reasonably free from weed seeds. No

provision is made in the Canada Grain Act for the classification of mixed grain. The following general rules for classification were adopted by the Inspection department for the guidance of inspectors, in Septemher, 1919, and have been in use ever since.
Mixed grain No. 1 shall consist of a mixture of wheat and oats, with wheat predominating.
Mixed grain No. 2 shall consist of a mixture of oats and wheat, oats predominating.
Mixed grain No. 3 shall consist of a mixture of wheat and barley, or barley and wheat.
Mixed grain No. 4 shall consist of a mixture of oats and barley, or barley and oats.
Other mixtures of grain, such as wheat" and rye, or rye and wheat, are classified as such.
5.	A survey could not be held on spelts as there is no provision for classification. A survey could be held on mixed grain.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill
has very recently come down and I have not had an opportunity of studying it in detail. As to the construction of the lines contemplated by the legislation I do not wish at the moment to raise any objection. But I do not want the second reading to pass without a protest against one feature of the legislation, a protest which I can carry into committee, but which I want to enter now because in my judgment it does affect in some degree the principle of the measure.
C.N.R.-Construction

In this bill, as I read it, the Governor in Council will be able to guarantee bonds of the Canadian National Railway, thus pledging the credit of Canada to such bonds as may be issued. By following this procedure the government will not come before parliament and ask for an appropriation in the estimates in the regular way, either for the provision of money direct or by way of guarantee. Hitherto the plan followed has been to include in the estimates the amounts representing the credit of the country, so far as it goes, extending to the road. This is only right: the nation should know, by one complete and clear statement, what the annual commitments are. We have been accustomed to getting that information from the estimates, and I am opposed to any scheme to submerge our commitments in some separate bill, thereby making impossible a fair comparison of the estimates of a given year with those of previous years. As I have suggested, I do not rise to object at all to such construction as may be deemed to be necessary; I rise to protest against the plan of the measure as introduced, enabling the administration to appear to be diminishing or contracting estimates when in fact they are not doing so. Why is clause 5 in the bill? Why does the government not have the matter dealt with in the regular way so that comparisons can be made and the country can know, from the production of the estimates for each year, what it faces in the way of expenditure and commitments for the next year? On a previous occasion, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will remember, I urged that the estimates should show separately and distinctly what was intended to be provided in cash and what by way of guarantee, and the Minister of Finance approved of the suggestion and promised to endeavour to work it out. I think that rule should apply to the estimates. Hitherto the entire vote, whether by guarantee or by express appropriation in cash, has been included in one'item or two or three different items, the guarantee and the cash not being distinguished. Nevertheless, we knew what the country's entire commitment was. On the other hand, if this bill passes, a large portion of the country's obligation for the year to come will be hidden away under the covers of this legislation and will not be disclosed in the estimates for the year.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Mr. Speaker, the
provision of money for public undertakings by legislation rather than by yearly estimate is not at all uncommon; I think I could refer

to several statutes of the s?me kind. One of the difficulties in this:	Amounts passed
each year in the estimates get through, say, in June; no money is available for work until after the session, and in the ensuing autumn very little can be accomplished. The bill states the entire estimated cost for three years, and when any of the railway estimates are up in the House, anything done or left undone in connection with this legislation can be discussed. Take the good roads movement: a certain bulk amount was voted for a number of years, but that did not deter the House from discussing in detail the
Was the amount not provided for it in the estimates each year?

The amount was not in the estimates; the discussion this year took place on the salaries of the officials. Under the statute the appropriation of that money was spread over a definite term of years; so it is in this case, except that we are dealing with railways, not highways. The purpose of the bill is not to hide anything or to keep anything from parliament; it is merely to enable the practical working out of the projects without delay. By this legislation the House says to the Canadian National Railway Board: Proceed for three years, up to a certain limit, in the construction of railway lines. As to the other point which my hon. friend had in mind, and concerning which his remarks were perfectly true, a portion of this expenditure would be by guarantee and a portion by direct vote through legislation, but by section 3 I think it is any lines of railway connecting with the government railways can be delivered by order in council to be government railways and be constructed out of the consolidated revenue. So there will be a distinct cleavage through the orders in council between those to be guaranteed and those to be paid out of consolidated revenue. I can assure the House that it is merely for the sake of expediting the construction that the legislation is brought down in this way. There will be no effort to hide any amount, only it is an amount for a three-year period instead of one year.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My experience is that railway subsidies, which are almost akin to this appropriation, are always voted separate from the estimates, so I think there is nothing unusual in this.
Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albc"*' T

C.N.R.-Construction
would like some explanation from the minister of this vote for providing money. I know that provincial governments when they guarantee the bonds of railway companies have always had this difficulty, that the bonds brought and always have brought a lower price even though with a government guarantee than they would if they were the direct issue of the government itself. That must obtain here, and I fail to see why something should be lost on the sale of the bonds when, after all, it is the credit of Canada that is at stake. The country must pay it, and I do not see why we should sell in a lower market when we can sell in a higher by making the bonds a direct obligation on the country'. That is all I want to say regarding that.
Despite some criticism I have seen in my province I think that the proposition, if it is carried out, of practically crossing New Brunswick with a railway will ultimately be a good thing, not for the southern portion of New Brunswick, but for the extreme eastern and central portions, and looking at it from the provincial standpoint I regard it as an excellent thing. I cannot understand, however, why it is not accompanied by the taking over of the St. John and Quebec railway and the completion of that line, which would give the government a network of railways over the province and relieve the province of a national undertaking which was imposed upon it because this parliament had cut the Transcontinental railway across New Brunswick in a place where it would be useful to no one, never has been useful and never will be useful, and a fertile section of the province was left without railway connection which is absolutely necessary. The province has to-day a very heavy load, a quarter of a million dollars a year, and it would be easy in a programme such as this for the government to take over that road and make it function along with the others.

I take it that this being a three-year programme for the railways, it is all we are to expect for a three-year period. In the first place, I think that the government ought to let us know what this year's programme is going to be and give us some idea how many of these things are going to be dangled in front of certain constituencies and not going to be gone on with. Let us know what railway construction is going to be done. This bill, as I see it, is a very convenient bill for my hon. friends from more than one standpoint. In the first place it gives them
a larger bunch of carrots to wave than they otherwise would have, and they like that.
In the next place, when we get down to an entirely different system of book-keeping in connection with the railways, it is going to be difficult for the House to institute any methods of comparison one way or the other. Indeed, apart from any matter of comparison, it is going to be difficult for the House even to keep track of what is going on. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways did point out that there were two distinct classo; of credit that would be used by the railways, there is the consolidated fund, and there is borrowing. So far as consolidated fund payments are concerned they would have to stand in a different position, he said, and I presume he meant they would have to be voted just as they arc now. But if the House is to have the satisfaction of getting some part of the definite particulars in connection with the annual vote, I would have thought it would have been better that the House should get them all.
Then again-I suppose we can deal with this when we are in committee-it looks i,o me as if the bill was drawn in such a way that irrespective of votes the treasury in some way or other was to be opened to the railways under this bill merely
4 p.m. looking to a subsequent repayment out of other loans. I do not know whether that is a point that has been considered by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but I do not believe if he h;,s considered it that he is going to agree with it.
Speaking to the principle of the bill, this being a three-year programme I would like to know if it means that the government have closed their eyes for a period of three years to other requests for railway construction work. Is this the government's programme for three years? I would just like to point out one thing in this connection and that is that the government as the owner of the railways, in addition to the position it occupies as such owner, having regard to the necessary construction to be done in order to enable the business of the country to be carried on, is also obligated contractually to certain construction. It is obligated in certain sections of this country, not by contractual relations I admit, but by work already done and by statements already made it is practically obligated to construction. Some of the items in to-day's bill of fare are obligated in that manner. I mean obligated by partial construction, by representations, and by people going into the district on the faith of the work that has been done and on these
C.N.R.-Construction

representations. They are mixed up with a three-year programme, and I think that the government ought to let us know whether these works that have already been started and on the faith of which people have gone into the country are going to be given the right of way in this three-year schedule.
Again, I point to the other class of construction, the class of construction that the government is bound to do as a matter of contract. I am going to mention in the first instance, and it is quite enough for my purpose, the viaduct in Toronto. There is not a single word of that in this three-year programme-not a word. I want to remind my hon. friends of this, Mr. Speaker. Speaking from recollection it is now something like eleven years, ten years at any rate, since the contract was signed to build a viaduct at Toronto, but so far the city has been unable to get anything whatever from the government. Last year a deputation waited upon the government, which very courteously promised serious consideration. Well they have got nothing yet, except that "serious consideration." I did not know this matter was coming up to-day. I am again speaking from memoiy and subject to correction, but my recollection is that on the faith of that agreement the city of Toronto has spent upwards of $26,000,000. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. I have no doubt these reports were made to him.

hon. member that the government, having taken over the Grand Trunk in the manner in which it took it over, is bound by ail the obligations of the Grand Trunk no matter what they amounted to?

The thing seems to be entirely preposterous. I am not talking for Toronto only. What is the matter, practically, with the whole of that large part of rural Ontario served by Toronto? Has my hon. friend ever been so unfortunate as to go into the Union Station and have to risk his life on the low levels?

But let that go; let us assume for a minute that there is some possible justification for the attitude that Toronto can get nothing. But what about the safety of the people generally? What about maintaining the frightful mantrap the minister is operating in Toronto to-day? Everybody knows that something ought to be done. I do not quite agree with the interpretation placed upon this matter by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), that this constitutes the government's railway programme for three years, because if such were the case, I think a great many sections of the country would be disappointed. Mr. J. FRED. JOHNSTON (Last Mountain) : I had intended to postpone my few remarks on this measure until we got into committee, but on account of what the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) have just said, I think probably this is the right place. On Section 2-Power to construct and complete lines described in schedule.
Would the minister prefer to discuss the details of the schedules at this stage, or later on?

I should like to ask the minister where the junction point will be between the Hanna-Warden branch and Lovema-Warden branch? Will they both run directly into Warden, or will the Hanna-Warden branch touch the Loverna line at some point south of Warden?

What is the reason for building the line from Hanna to Warden? Perhaps I should explain to the minister my reason for asking this question. It is mainly to shorten
the haul of coal to Hanna and points east.

Ls it the
intention of the railway directors now to change the divisional point from Big Valley to Warden?

just now. We shall need to operate the line first. It may be better to leave it as it is, or it may be deemed wise to make the change. It is a matter of operation.

I wish to
protest, basing my protest on my knowledge of the conditions there, against the change of the divisional point from Big Valley to Warden. There is every facility at Big Valley for a divisional point, whereas at Warden there are none of thes'e facilities. I want information with
respect to one of the branches' which it is proposed to build under this legislation, as it happens to lie wholly within the constituency I have the honour to represent. I am referring to Meductic, New Brunswick, westerly to the international boundary. The Minister, of course, is aware that the government to-day does not own the railway extending up and down the St. John Valley, of which this would be a branch, but operates it under a contract with the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, the stock of which is owned by the provincial government. This, as no doubt the minister is also aware, is not by any means a new scheme, but was originated when the government railways were being operated by Mr. Gutelius; and it was intended to give the railway lines in New Brunswick an independent outlet to the United States, making them
independent of the Canadian Pacific Railwa3-to which company all the traffic originating on the government lines' in the province of New Brunswick and destined for New England points is at the present time handed over. The arrangement has been commended by railway men of experience who have looked into it. But I want to point out that there are certain considerations which the government, in providing the money for the construction of the line, and the management of the Canadian National Railways in putting their seal of approbation on the project, should bear very positively in mind. The first consideration to which I allude is this, that this line should not be built until it is determined with definiteness, and after the very greatest possible care has been exercised, as to who is to build the extension to the boundary line between New Brunswick and the Maine Central railway. And one question I desire to ask now is, with what connection is this branch line to be yoked up? What railway company, what body of men, are building from the boundary to the Maine Central connection, which I understand is to be some miles west of Vanceboro? If it is to be the company known as the Eastern Maine Railway Company I want to ask the minister to have a care before making any arrangement or entering into any contract with that company. While I would be the last one to do any injury to any promotion of that character in the state of Maine, I have very considerable doubt as to the ability of that company actually to build its lines. I do not think that this branch line should be undertaken until the Canadian National Railway directorate is assured not only of the bona fides but of the financial ability of the parties to build the connecting link that will be necessary. I have heard it rumoured within the last few weeks that the government itself is to build the part that is to lie within the state of Maine. I cannot credit that rumour because no provision has been made here for such work, and in fact I do not think it would be a very good policy. But there are a few other considerations to which I would call the attention of the minister. If the Canadian National Railways are to build the connecting link on this side-and I believe that in the end it will be good business-there are two other things that should be taken into account. First, they should extend the St. John and Quebec Railway to Grand Falls on the Transcontinental as originally contemplated, in order that it may get the business originating in northern New Brunswick; and, in the second place, it should rebuild the railway
C.N.R.-Cons true tion

bridge of Fredericton which was built by the late Senator Temple, the promoter and owner of the Canada Eastern Railway now part of the government railway system and which is wholly inadequate to bear the traffic of modern locomotives. These two things seem desirable. Another question which I wish to ask the minister is of much importance. Is it contemplated that the work shall be started this year, or is it to be held over until the eve of the next general election? I am very much interested in that question personally, as the minister can very well understand. I will tell him now that it will not get him any votes to hold the matter over another year, while it might get him votes if he started it now. I want him to be sure alsp that the Maine connection is a bona fide one.
The last question in regard to the election is important.
It is important to me personally.

The government has no
desire, nor has the Canadian National board, ;o use any of the lines at the time of construction for political purposes. There is nothing of the kind in my mind, because if I were undertaking any of this work for political purposes I would build lines in other places before I would do anything in some of these districts.
What about the Hudson Bay?
It is not contemplated to do much work this year. We shall do the surveys and twenty-five miles of grading.
Only the surveys this year?

That is about all you can do this year the season being far gone already. With regard to the question of my hon. friend concerning the connecting up of the railway with the United States, this branch on the Canadian side is to be constructed only on the distinct undertaking that the line on the other side will be built to meet it, and I think I can tell my hon. friend that the work will not be begun until such time as the Canadian National board has assurance that those who take up the work will be financially in a position to carry it through.
Has the minister information as to who is to build the American end of this line, or is there any definite proposition before the management with regard to it?
Not at the present time.

The building of No. 6,
the I.ong Lake branch, shortens the distance between Toronto and Winnipeg quite materially, and I have no doubt that freight from the Grand Trunk Pacific can be sent down this branch instead of coming via the head of the lakes, thus lessening operating cost. I have no criticism to offer in this regard. At the same time, there would be perhaps an inclination on the part of the management to switch along this loop the daily passenger train running over the Canadian National via Port Arthur, Fort William, Fort Frances, Rainy River and other points. The section of the Canadian National line to which I refer serves at least one hundred thousands people, and I would urge that very serious consideration should be given before diverting this passenger train and so inconveniencing the people along the present route. If the utilization of the Long Lake branch would improve the passenger service and cut down operating expenses, I do not know that the people at the head of the lakes and the rest of the district would object, but personally I doubt very much a there would be really any saving to the system by diverting this passenger train from its present route. I would suggest to the government that before any change is made they should thoroughly investigate the operating costs and the traffic returns of the train which serves more than a hundred thousand people, because it would be both injurious to that section of the country and to the railroad itself from the financial standpoint if a change of route were decided upon.

It is disappointing on looking over the schedule not to find included the extension of the St. John and Quebec railway to Grand Falls. If the minister holds the view that this is to be practically the list of construction for the next three years, I trust that he will draw to the attention of the directors of the National Railways the importance of this extension, for it involves only a few miles of construction and would accomplish more than any similar length of railway that might be built in the near future. Another matter I would draw the minister's attention to is the lack of station accommodation at St. John. Beyond the site there is practically nothing there in the way of a station, and passengers are unprotected from the weather. The people have been very patient regarding this condition of affairs, wishing that perhaps even more urgent works should be undertaken first, but at last they feel that something should be done and that to allow the present condition to continue

With regard to No. 10, " Thunderhill line, northwesterly to Prince Albert branch," will the minister indicate which branch is termed the Prince Albert branch, and what point is to be the terminus?
Before replying to my hon. friend, perhaps the minister might give some information on the points I have raised before they escape his memory?

The extension of the terminals at St. John is being considered by the Railway department in connection with the Public Works department, it being essential from the railway point of view that certain things be done at the harbour, which will make it easier to determine just what ought to be done in the way of railroad terminals. As to the Quebec and St. John railway, it belongs to a private company, and this year the charter was renewed for another term.
The line is leased to the government. The completion of these few miles would connect the railway with the Transcontinental. The Transcontinental could build the connection.

But you are building a branch from the St. John and Quebec railway to the Maine border, and this branch does not touch the government end of the railway at all, nor the leased line.

I think there is a
stronger argument for the completion of the St. John and Quebec Railway so that it will connect with the Transcontinental. Has the
minister anything to say in reference to increased accommodation-warehouses and so on-for tiie railway business?

That has all been considered by the board. The government would not care to make an announcement concerning these things, as to what ought to be done and when it ought to be done, except on recommendation of the board.

I would like to say a few words in regard to item No. 3 in the schedule, to which reference has been made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for St. Johu (Mr. MacLaren). I am a little disappointed to hear the minister say there is no agreement with the Eastern Maine or any other railway to build their share of the connecting link between the Eastern Maine Railway and the St. John and Quebec Railway. As long ago as 1920 I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways of that day and arranged a meeting between him and representatives of the Eastern Maine Railway and the St. John and Quebec Railway. The then Minister of Railways was very much impressed with the plans that were under consideration. I believe that preliminary surveys had been made and an estimate prepared some years ago of the cost, and the railway men who had it under review regarded the project very favourably indeed. The then Minister of Railways asked the representatives of the Eastern Maine Railway what guarantee we would have that they would build their section of the road in Maine if we built ours. I am speaking from memory now, but I think my recollection is correct. The representatives of the Eastern Maine Railway said: "We will give you better than a guarantee; if you will agree to build your portion of the line in 1921 we will build our portion of it this year; that is, we will do our work one year ahead of yours." So I think that the Minister of Railways or the general manager of the Government Railways should have no difficulty in making an arrangement under which the Maine portion of the road would be built; in fact, I understand that the offer still holds good. As to the completion of the St. John and Quebec Railway to Grand Falls there can be no difference of opinion as to the advisability of taking that step. In fact, that should be the logical outcome of the building of the connecting link mentioned in this schedule, because otherwise you will have to bring the traffic from northern New Brunswick and eastern Quebec over the

C.N.R.-C onstruction

Transcontinental to McGivney Junction around by Fredericton-a very roundabout route indeed. The portion of country north of Centreville through which the St. John and Quebec Railway has been projected is without railway facilities, though it is a very fertile and productive farming district, to say nothing of the through traffic that originates on the Transcontinental in northern New Brunswick and Quebec. Another point that has not been touched on is the necessity for the construction of a ten mile section between St. John and Westfield. If we build this necessary connecting link from Meductic westerly to the international bounary to give an outlet to the United States-for that is the object of it-it will be necessary also to build that ten mile section between St. John and Westfield. At present we are paying for running rights over that section of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have endeavoured time and again, without success, to get particulars as to the agreement under which those running rights are granted; I understand that the charge is fairly heavy, and that is one of the reasons why the deficit on the St. John and Quebec Railway has been so large. I pointed out to the minister a few days ago when his estimates were up that owing to lack of siding facilities, freight which originates on the St. John and Quebec Railway and arrives at West St. John has to go across the reversible falls to East St. John and back. A toll of one and a half cents per hundred pounds each way has to be paid on this freight. Then I believe we pay the Canadian Pacific Railway a switching charge of three cents per hundred pounds, whereas if we had proper facilities on the west side of the river we could do the switching there ourselves. I believe we own the tracks and the docks at West St. John, yet we have to pay the Canadian Pacific to do the switching for us. The member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) tells me we do not own the tracks. Well, that is worse still-we certainly should own them. This situation is most unheard of, and it surely should be remedied in the near future. The connecting link which is now to be built is a project which I have urged on the department very strongly every year I have been here, and I am pleased to see that the work is at last to be undertaken. However, I would strongly urge upon the minister that he consider very seriously the taking over of the St. John and Quebec Railway from the government of New Brunswick. It is the only railway in the Maritime provinces that has not been taken over; it is at 
present operated under lease by the Dominion government. This road is needed to round out the system of National railwa}^ in the Maritimes, especially in view of the building of the connecting link mentioned in this schedule.

With your kind permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks relative to item No. 4 of the schedule appended to this bill. In this measure brought down by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), it is proposed to add 995 miles to our National railway system. Of these 995 miles, 856 will be built in the West; this fact has afforded an opportunity to one of our hon. colleagues representing the city of Toronto, to say with a good deal of truth to our western friends, that they would be wrong to doubt our good intentions and generosity towards them, since we are ready to vote them, without any hesitation, a sum of $21,000,000 for railways in which they are specially concerned. Out of the 139 miles in which the East is interested, the province of Quebec is given for its share 14 miles of new railway. I do not rise as a protest against this small proportion allowed to my province, but on the contrary, to rejoice in the fact that the 14 miles in question are all to be found in my home district. Indeed, I have the advantage of living at the entrance of the Laurentian hills, that chain of mountains whose wealth and beauty are, each day, becoming better known. The surest way to get returns from this capital which that mountainous country, rightly called a second Switzerland, represents to us, is to build good roads, construct railways that will facilitate reaching this landscape of indescribable beauty and penetrate into this paradise of tourists. The Canadian Pacific Railway has, for a number of years, traversed the Laurentian hills. The Canadian National previously known as the Great 'Northern Railway, reaches it also at St. Jerome and extends as far as Huberdeau. However, there has never existed up to now a direct line from Montreal to these beautiful mountains. Notwithstanding that this part of the Laurentides is at least as delightful as the one which the Canadian Pacific Railway crosses, the former contains numerous lakes, magnificent forests and most picturesque mountains. Some of these local places have become famous, namely, the Lake of the Sixteen Islands, comparing favourably with the most beautiful Laurentian lakes; Arundel, Huberdeau, through which the Rouge flows and called " the Garden of the Laurentides," by Cure Labelle, the first pioneer of this beau-

C.N.R.-C onstruction
tiful region. The wealth and prosperity of a province contribute to the wealth and prosperity of the whole country; that is why, sir, I consider, that the Laurentides are a national asset for Canada. This part of the country, to-day, is beginning to be better appreciated; the influential press recognizes, describes and praises the charms of the Lauren tian hills. For the last twenty-five years, in my own humble sphere, I have praised their most picturesque attractions, highly commended the advantages of the sports to those wishing to settle there, and proclaiming as well their natural wealth, the farming and industrial development of tviia remarkable region situated to the north of Montreal. The Laur-entian mountains have been advertised first, by means of the railway', then the motor car and finally by the building of good roads, and all have contributed in drawing an ever-increasing flow of tourists. The Montreal and Mont Laurier highway started by the provincial government and subsidized by the Dominion Government, is being completed. In a few months, we shall be able to travel from Montreal to Ste. Agathe on an almost perfect road. The latter will, before long, be further extended to Mont Laurier. It is also said that another road will be built in the county of Argenteuil, from Lachute to Arundel, and will join the road connecting Mont Laurier, Ste. Agathe and Montreal with the Canadian Pacific trains already packed with travellers; and the Canadian National, once connected to Montreal, Mil also have numerous tourists, these together with the improvement of roads, will lead to twice even thrice the number of tourists directing themselves towards the Laurentian hills.
Without ever losing sight that farming, colonization, industry and the development of the ore fields will greatly benefit from the easier and more rapid transportation facilities in a region which contains in its natural state vast wealth and numerous hopes, I wish to especially point out the great benefit that the country may derive from the Laurentides in the way of sport, summer resorts and touring trips, should access to our mountains and lakes be made easier to the lovers of beautiful vistas. It would be a great pity to leave unknown and untouched scenery like that which abounds in the Laurentian hills, to the north of the Metropolis of Canada. We would be displaying an ignorance of the true nature of things if we allowed any further our tourists to transfer to other lands, especially to the United States, millions of dollars each year, owing to our not making easy the means of access to the mountains which are in no way inferior to those of our neighbours to the
275i
south in regard to beauty of landscape and abundance of game. With railways and good roads, not only shall we keep in our province Canadians that leave it during the summer season, but we shall draw here hundreds of American tourists anxious to visit our mountains. The mountainous regions in Europe, as well as those of the United States, have become prosperous owing to the influx of tourists that railways and good roads attract to these places. Take as an instance Switzerland; the Adirondacks, the White mountains, in the United States, and many others. What has been done in Switzerland, in France, in the United States, Canada must and shall accomplish. The Government has thrown the foundation of this project; they must persevere, carry it out without delay, and that is what they are doing. Then only will they be in a position to offer to the curiosity and admiration of travellers in this enchanted country, a scenery nowhere else equalled. Indeed, I again state, no country offers a more picturesque concourse of mountains, lakes, cascades and forests filled with game, the whole enclosed in an immense territory offering the most pleasing variety of views, to which the traveller may find easy access, providing railways and good roads are placed at his disposal. There may be found in other parts more lofty mountains, deeper ravines, thicker forests but nowhere will there be found a country more filled with thrills, more serene landscapes, sports easier of enjoyment and a more agreeable sojourn than in these mountains. Along this Laurentian route which stretches from Montreal to Ste. Agathe, by way of the Canadian Pacific, and which, before long, will reach from Montreal to the Lake of the Sixteen Islands and Huberdeau, by way of the Canadian National, along this Laurentian route, I say, which is opening up on stretches of hundreds and hundreds of miles, at times parallel to the river Du Nord, at times skirting sky-coloured lakes, and still at other times winding along a mountain or traversing refreshing forests, one may choose among the most picturesque sites which doft i.t here and there throughout its length, those that are conspicuous either for their ru.Tie beauty or for their special features more in harmony with each one's taste. A tent is put up, a bungalow or a sumptuous villa is built according to one's inclinations and here is the ideal spot already found to rest and live in peace, far from the worries of strenuous life and close to one's place of business; conditionally, of course, on there being a good road or railway to reach the spot.
By building the 12 miles which appear in the schedule submitted, that is to say, from
C.N.R.-C (instruction

Grande-Freniere to Rinfret Junction, in other words, from St. Eustache to St. Jerome, the Government ensures a direct communication between Montreal and these parts which I have just mentioned, a region that is not only one of the most beautiful as regards variety of scenery but which is equally one of the richest in natural resources. In fact, this territory contains immense possibilities in farming, the same may be said of its industry and mining. Lumber of the best quality is to be found there, the dairy industry is highly developed, a number of carloads of cheese are weekly exported via the Canadian National Railway; mfeca, graphite and other minerals have lately been discovered in that part of the country. In a word, this portion of the Laurentides which is in the county of Argenteuil, is no less beautiful and rich than are the regions which the Canadian Pacific traverses and better known because the trains of that railway reach it directly from Montreal. It is most astonishing that the Canadian National which traverses this enchanted part of the Laurentian hills is not yet directly connected with Montreal. Travellers are forced to travel by the Canadian Pacific, to a junction called Montfort, near St. Jerome, where they change trains to take the Canadian National. It is a serious drawback for tourists. So far as traffic is concerned-and it is considerable-both freight and express trains must pass through Joliette to reach Montreal, that is to say, a distance of 74 miles from St. Jerome. When the projected line from Grand-Freniere to Rinfret Junction, about 12 miles, shall be built, the distance from St. Jerome to ' Montreal will only be 30 miles. One may imagine the inestimable advantages that will result from this line both for tourists and traffic, as St. Jerome is the centre through which passes all the traffic coming from the north of the counties of Argenteuil and La-belle, served by the Canadian National railway. Moreover, St. Jerome has a population of 7,000 inhabitants and its trade is considerable. The transportation of products and goods from Montreal to the north or vice versa, at present controlled by the Canadian National, is effected by a 74-mile route instead of 30 which it will be when the branch line in question appearing at No. 4 of this schedule is constructed. The Canadian National is, however, one of the Government railways concerning which we deplore those enormous deficits. Well, I have no hesitation in saying that through the operation of this new line, which will directly connect the north with Montreal, the Canadian National will realize profits that will contribute to diminish, in a
'Mr. Prevost.]
small way perhaps, but nevertheless in an appreciable ratio, the deficits that we are bound, though regretfully, to admit. When the Canadian National reaches the Laurentides, by way of the branch line in question, when this link between the Metropolis and the Laurentian hills has been established, this line will give as much return as does the Canadian Pacific Railway in the north. It is more than 30 years since the Canadian Pacific inaugurated its line in the Laurentides. It proved a success from the start. It is ever so long that this branch line has been considered as one of those that give the best returns to that company. The same will be said of the Canadian National, when direct communication between Montreal and the Laurentides has been established.
Mr. Chairman, whoever has at heart the general interest of the country will be pleased to approve of this project which will, at last, connect by a state railway the northern parts of Montreal to the Metropolis. One last word, I hope that all the branch lines appearing in the schedule submitted to us may be as useful and timely as this one.

I might say in two or three words that I appreciate the beautiful description of the fine country to which my hon. friend refers. I have been there, and found it a little difficult to get in as rapidly as I wanted to, and difficult to get out rapidly at the particular time I wished to. I think, perhaps, it was late in the evening. Any person who has looked over that section of country will see the disadvantage of the Canadian National Railway in not having a direct connection with Montreal; and while the building of this section to which my hon. friend so eloquently referred would be a good thing for that portion of the country, I am sufficiently hard-hearted to say that I think :t will pay real money to the Canadian National Railways over and above all cost of operation.

I wonder if the minister could give me any assurance that the work on the Okanagan branch-No. 27 on the schedule-will be carried forward this year? This branch has now been something like eleven years under construction. I th:nk if ever there was a people who had a right to invoke the proposition that hope deferred maketh the heart sick it is the residents of that district. In conversation with the president and some of the officials of the National Board this year, they very cordially agreed with me when I made the statement that in Canada there would not be a better feeder

C .N.R-C onstruction
for the Canadian National Railway than the Kamloops-Okanagan branch. It embraces one of the most beautiful as well as one of the most fertile parts of Canada; and if the war had not intervened I have no doubt its completion would have been a matter of history several years ago. It must be remembered rhat, as a revenue producer, a line running through a horticultural section has many advantages over a line traversing a grain-growing portion of the country. Although it may take from thirty to fifty acres to produce a carload of grain, perhaps two acres or less of horticultural land will fill a car with fruit or vegetables. The member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) could speak better than I can from personal knowledge of the easterly end of this section. But coming down a little further towards my own home, we pass through the Falkland and Salmon river district, both of which are capable of great development. In Falkland there is the largest shipment on the continent probably awaiting transportation facilities. In the Salmon river district they have large lime deposits and great timber resources; and the district from that point to Armstrong is a very fertile agricultural district indeed. From Vernon the branch spur runs 16 miles to Lumby, one of the most progressive districts in our country, and the hinterland of that section contains untold wealth in the way of timber and minerals. Down the Okanagan lake to Kelowna it runs through a section that produces about two-thirds of the 5,000 cars of freight which are sent out in the season. It can easily be seen that this will be a great feeder to the Canadian National, once it is in operation. I would like to be able, if possible, to convey to the residents of this district the assurance that they will not have to wait another year before it is completed.

I would not like to go that far. The hon. member asks the question, and expects me to answer, I suppose. The closing words of my hon. friend's remarks were very succinct. He asks that he be given the assurance that the road will be completed this year. I think he scarcely meant that. The work is going to proceed, but owing to the fact that the season is very far advanced, although there are many miles already graded on that line, it would be hardly possible to finish it this year.
Could the assurance be given-and I think it might reasonably be done-that before another fruit crop is ready :o ship, the line will be completed?
I think that is the hope of the board.

Just a word in connection with this line. I do not think the Canadian National line will have a feeder, west of Edmonton, anything like the Kamloops-Kelowna line when it is completed. In my opinion that line, within a year after completion, will not only be paying interest and operation expenses, but it will furnish a good revenue to the Canadian National Railways. There has been some opposition to this road, but no person who has the best interest of the Canadian National Railways at heart has anything to say against this line. Indeed, I think that it is the people who are interested in the Canadian Pacific Railway who are circulating this propaganda that it would be money wasted. The Canadian Pacific Railway and its officials know the amount of freight that road will take from their railway. Not only will it be a benefit to the Canadian National in getting freight, but it will be a benefit to the farmers in the prairies in that it will give them direct connection with the Okanagan. The railway will be able to take grain from the prairies down to the coast, and the same cars can be loaded with fruit on the return trip. It will work both ways, and I would like to see that line completed with the least possible delay.
I wonder if I could recall the minister's mind to the question I asked a little time ago. Perhaps while he is travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific he could rest half-way and give me an answer.
What was the question?

Regarding the Thunderhill branch, which runs northwesterly to a point on the Prince Albert line. I asked him, what branch is termed the Prince Albert branch, and what is the terminus of the Thunderhill branch?

Largely the location of the line depends on the possibility of two things, the traffic and the engineering difficulties. This is the information that is given to me. There are four miles of the line graded. We propose to grade 17 miles in 1923 and to lay 21 miles of track. In 1925, it is proposed to lay track on the line for 23 miles at an estimated cost of $368,000, thus completing the line to tie into our Prince Albert main line near Tisdale.

Thai, then, is not the survey that was originally made, and that it had been expected would be fol-

lowed in connecting up with the Humboldt-Melfort line?
No, it is not.

Would the minister give
the general route of the Thunderhill branch?

The route of that line
has not been finally determined.
What is the intention?
I have given it as nearly as possible. The line must have been surveyed, because four miles of that particular line have been graded.
The minister has his engineers in front of him, and he might inform the committee what, in general, is the route proposed to be traversed by this line between the two termini.
From the present terminus, generally speaking, it takes a northerly direction to Tisdale.
What points does it touch?
I do not know that.

Could the minister get
that information?
We could get the information approximately, but it might not touch those points at all when the final survey is made. It may be impossible to touch the points I might name.

I have no
objection whatever to the branch that the minister proposes to run in a northwesterly direction from Kelvington to Tisdale, I believe would be the point. I would like, however, to call his attention to the fact that although that branch is needed there, I do not know why it should be called the Thunderhill branch. I am not sure when the Thunderhill branch was first surveyed. There have been a number of surveys since 1908, and the district between the end of the steel at Kelvington and the point north of Humboldt where it was anticipated that would meet another branch of the Canadian National railways, has been settled, some of it, at least, for fifteen or sixteen years in anticipation that that road would come through. This would seem as if the Thunderhill branch had been abandoned and a new branch has been named the Thunderhill branch. There are two soldier settlements that can well be served by the branch proposed by the minister, and I would not suggest that it should not be built. But I wish to voice a most emphatic objection to the abandoning of the 
old route which has been surveyed. I do not know the definite route, but it runs generally in a westerly direction from Kelvington to Lake Lenore, or possibly Wakaw.

I think I am fairly familiar with that country, and while what my hon. friend has said with regard to the western extension of the Thunderhill line is quite true, its construction has been delayed so long that several railways have been built ahead of it. I refer more particularly to the Grand Trunk north to Prince Albert, upon which Wakaw is situated. Then there is the Humboldt-Melfort line, and I think the Canadian Pacific has also a line in there somewhere. Therefore, there was no necessity for extending this line through the original route, for the reasons I have indicated. Accordingly, they have swung north and tied up with the Prince Albert line near Tisdale, connecting up those large soldier settlements The change was unavoidable on account ol those developments. Was the minister able to give any consideration to the request I made a few days ago when this matter was under discussion on the resolution, in regard to the reinstatement of the Bruederheim line in this schedule?

I thought I answered that pretty fully the other day. I pointed out that there were many lines on a tentative list, but there were altogether too many to be undertaken at one time. The Canadian National board was asked to revise its list, and the line to which my hon. friend refers, in not in the latest list. Some hon. gentleman has asked me if this means that nothing is to be done during the next three years except the lines mentioned in the schedule. Does the minister think that remark would apply to No. 2, the Sunny Brae-Guysborough branch, a line of 67 miles of railway proposed to cost $3,500,000, a line that has been promised more by political candidates in Nova Scotia than any other line of railway that I have ever heard of. What is the justification for spending $3,500.-

000 in building a line from Sunny Brae to Guysborough? That is not in the same place.

No, but it was in the district of my good friend the then Prime Minister. It was constructed. I did not, however, suggest this line. The board suggested this line to me without any suggestion on my part directly or indirectly, as all the lines were recommended to me. I think they must know what they are about.
