To hon. members of this
House who have been in the last two or three parliaments, the Guysborough railway question is a very familiar one; but as there are many hon. members present who were not in the last parliaments, perhaps I should take up a few moments in explaining the question.
I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) is one of those in the present House who should receive some information in connection with the matter. In the session of 1910, this resolution was passed in this House by both of the then parties, Conservatives and Liberals:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived in the commercial and industrial development of the province of Nova Scotia, when the Intercolonial Railway of Canada should be extended into the nonrailway counties of the eastern section of the province.
I am of course interested in this matter and probably it will be considered that anything I say in behalf of the interests of Guysborough must be more or less exaggerated. But I can tell the House that the county of Guysborough has never had any railway except the service of a few miles in the extreme northeastern section of that large county. This is one of the largest counties of the province, extending along the sea coast from Halifax county down to the strait of Canso a hundred and fifty miles, all consisting of the best fishing grounds that are to be found in the whole Dominion. The fishing business is undeveloped because there are no facilities; and the timber limits in the county are quite extensive. These resources would contribute traffic to a railway for very many years to come, and in addition the agricultural districts of the county are second to none while the undeveloped mineral resources of Guysborough have great possibilities.. But apart from all these, I would mention particularly the fact that Country Harbour in this county is one of the best harbours in the world. I see my hon. friend from York laughing.
I was not laughing.

Well, the hon. member
was smiling at any rate. But I do not want him to take my word on that point. I will read from Hansard a speech delivered by Sir Robert Borden in the session of 1910 with reference to this very subject. At page 1182 of Hansard of that year Sir Robert Borden is reported as follows:
I passed along the shore of the county of Halifax to the county of Guysboro last summer. I travelled altogether about 500 miles through districts not served by railways at all, and where railway development would mean a great deal to the people and lead to considerable development in that little province. I can tell the Minister of Railways-
C.N.R.-C (instruction

The present Minister of Railways, (Mr. Graham) was minister then too.
-a great many things I saw, I could speak of a great many districts where railway facilities might mean a great deal to the people, and might lead to very great progress and advancement in that little province. I saw, in the county of Guysboro,-
I would ask the hon. member for York (Mr. Hanson) to note that.
-just across the line from the county of Halifax, one of the most splendid harbours that can be found anywhere in the world-Country Haibour. This harbour stretches back 10 miles from its mouth, with water close up to the shore everywhere from forty-five to sixty feet in depth, landlocked twice, and with a splendid roadstead outside where, in almost any weather, ships can ride in safety-and have ridden in safety-without going inside. And in what condition did I find the place? Not more than a dozen families are living around that harbour. There was no railway development, no opportunity for commerce, and the fishermen had gone to the adjoining Isaac's Harbour or Fisherman's Harbour, for the reason that these smaller harbours would subserve their purposes better than this magnificent Country Harbour of which I have spoken. All along that shore are opportunities of development. The people of Hailfax county, and those of other counties in the province of Nova Scotia to which allusion has been made, have, it seems to me, fairly good reason to complain that their interests in respect of railway development, have not been properly attended to in the past.
He concluded:
This is no time for hesitation and vaccilation. Make up your mind-and I hope you have made it up in the direction I have indicated then give to the Intercolonial railway the branches, feeders, extensions which would be given, if it were owned by any of the great railway corporations.
That is what Sir Robert Borden had to say on this subject in 1910. The House unanimously passed the resolution and in the year 1911 the government called for tenders for this very road covering a distance of 67 miles. At the same time, they called for tenders for another road in the county of Halifax extending from Dartmouth eastwards to Musquodoboit. These tenders were called for at the time of the election of 1911) but unfortunately for the government, and for the county of Guysborough, and Canada as well, the Liberals went out of power and the Conservatives came in. What happened0 The government of Sir Robert Borden cancelled the proposed contract for this particular railway in the county of Guysborough and proceeded with a railway in that gentleman's own county. Well, I suppose he was perfectly right in going on with a railway in his constituency, but I say that it was unfair to cancel the contract for this railway, simply because a Liberal was returned to represent the county of Guysborough. That was in 1911 and nothing has been done since in connection with this matter. The question was brought up year fMr. Mclsaac.]
after year by the representative of that constituency, Mr. Sinclair, while the Conservative party was in power. When Hon. Frank Cochrane was Minister of Railways, he returned the same answer to Mr. Sinclair ou every occasion, that the government was looking into the matter, and hoped to build the Guysborough railway at an early date. The work however, was never undertaken and I have every reason therefore at this time to congratulate the present Minister of Railwavs, on the step he is about to take. I brought the matter to the attention of the late Minister of Railways, Mr. Kennedy, the first time I saw him on his only official tour of the province of Nova Scotia. I represented to him the rank injustice that had been done the county of Guysborough in ignoring for so many years its undoubted claim to a railway. That honourable gentleman promised consideration of the claim of Guysborough, but unfortunately he did not live long enough to bring the matter before the House. So that I am more than pleased to congratulate the present minister on his dicision to carry out the recommendation of the board to give to that county a railway to which it is entitled and of which it has been deprived for so long.
This line will be a splendid feeder to the Intercolonial railway. In 1911 before tenders were called for, another branch line known as the Sunny Brae branch from Ferrona to Sunny Brae a distance of 12 miles, a completed road, was purchased by the government of that day from a private company. The sum of $100,000 was paid by the then government for this branch, and in addition to that they spent between 885,000 and 8100,000 in surveys. This was all done in 1911 for the purpose of extending the road from Sunny Brae to Guysborough to connect up with Country Harbour, which as Sir Robert Borden himself stated is one of the best harbours in the world. It is open the year round, and if this branca line is extended to connect up with it the result will be a shortening of the distance to European ports. I have heard hon. gentlemen on the Progressive side speak of the advantage of the Transcontinental railway down in Quebec, because it shortens the distance by about 200 miles in the shipment of freight from the West to the seaport. This would shorten the distance still further by about 50 or 75 miles. No branch of the Intercolonial railway was ever built that would prove of greater benefit not only to the county it will serve, but also to the railway general Iv, for this railway besides providing much-needed facilities for Guysborough would also be a great

C.N.R.-Construction
feeder to the Canadian National Railway, so that it would be advantageous all round. Th; Minister of Railways is now going to see that justice, long deferred, is done to Guysborough, and I congratulate him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the programme which the minister has brought down for the construction of branch railways interests me considerably. For many years certain sections of Nova Scotia, in addition to that portion which is so worthily represented by my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Mclsaac), have been in need of further railway advantages. In 1901 a company undertook the construction of a railway to the southern shore of the island of Cape Breton from the strait of Canso to the historic town of Louisburg. Thirty miles was constructed from Point Tup-per to St. Peter's, and was operated as a branch railway until 1919, when I think the late government purchased it from the owners and it has since been operated in conjunction with the Canadian National Railways. I desire to point out to the minister what it was my privilege to bring to his attention years ago when he held his present portfolio, and that is the necessity for constructing the line from St. Peter's to Louisburg. As is well known, Louisburg is the only open winter port on the southern shore of Cape Breton through which Newfoundland traffic passes. Unfortunately during the winter months the harbour of Sydney is usually blocked with ice floes so that passenger and freight traffic from Newfoundland has to be diverted to Louisburg. But on disembarking at Louisburg passengers have no railway accommodation except a coal train running to Sydney, where it connects with the Canadian National Railways. Of course, it is well known that the historic town of Louisburg was a very important military post during the French regime. It is now an important fishing centre.
We are suffering very much in eastern Canada, particularly in Nova Scotia, under prevailing conditions. When I heard my good friends from the West speaking of the hard times in their constituencies, I was inclined to make comparisons between western and eastern conditions. Without wishing to minimize in the slightest degree the conditions described by them, I beg to assure my hon, friends from the West that conditions in Nova Scotia today call for as favourable treatment as is required in any other part of the Dominion. I shall not go into the reasons in detail and so delay the progress of this bill. I have listened with very much interest to the minister's answer to the question put to him by several hon. members opposite as to whether or not
this programme constituted all the railway construction during the next three years. Neither last session nor this have I pressed for the construction of this railway, because I had reason to believe that the financial conditions were not such as to justify any new construction. But the magnificent and varied programme of railway construction in western Canada satisfies me that the government has overcome its greatest difficulties with regard to finances and finds itself in a position to undertake further railway construction. Therefore I would remind the minister that my constituency is very much in need of this branch line.
I serve notice upon him now that at an early date in the next session I shall renew this request in the expectation that provision will be made for the construction of this railway in the Supplementary, if not in the Main Estimates next year.

In regard to Nos. 11 and 12, both short branch lines, I should like to have the minister's assurance that these will be completed this year. The Paddockwood line is practically all graded, the other line, the Melford branch, is partially graded, and the people to be served by these branches are very anxious to have some assurance that steel will be laid this year. The Paddockwood line runs through a district which was largely settled by soldiers, and was mentioned in the report brought down by the Pensions board last year.

It would be foolish for the minister to give assurances of what can be done this year. However, there will be some work done on these lines. I hope they will be completed, but I cannot bind the board or the construction company. The best that can be done will be done.
What is really meant? On the one hand we are told that the work and financing will be spread over a three-year period; then on the other hand we hear that it is not anything of the kind.
My hon. friend's memory is short; I did not say that it was not anything of the kind.
No, other members say so and you say nothing.
Silence is golden sometimes. I did say a few moments ago that parliament is supreme, that while this is a three-year programme parliament can do anything.
What is the real intention?

We hope to have this
programme completed three years. I can
C.N.R.-C onstruction

readily see some reason for my hon. friend's statement, because in looking over this carefully I see nothing to confine the programme to three years. I propose to move an amendment to insert in the second line of section 2 certain words which I have handed to the Chairman, to make it clear that it is- a chree-year programme.

I do not know that that helps us very much. We are trying to find out what is the real intention of the government. Of course Darliament can turn the government out-very likely it would if it were at all wise.

That would be a bad
thing.
Does the government now declare that this programme represents their railway construction for the next three years?
I did not say that at all.
I am trying to find out what the fact is.

Perhaps my hon. friend
will listen carefully this time. I said that parliament can do anything it likes'-

We have that
already.

-and that the government can introduce anything it likes. As I pointed out a few minutes ago, if it is thought wise to have the Canadian National Board select the most pressing cas-es out of several hundred and give us a three-year construction programme, that does not mean that there will be no other work undertaken during that three years. Nobody is bound by this three-year programme being absolutely definite.
Then I take it that it is a three-year programme which you may depart from as much as you like.

As much as parliament
likes.

We will have to leave it at that. What are the business reasons for the Sunny Brae branch? We have had the political ones from various politicians interested as well as their advice.
I ask for the engineering and traffic reports on this proposed line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not suppose that in the case of any projected railway a report could be produced showing it is going to pay right away. Every enterprise of this character

has to depend for its justification either upon an expectation of early succes-s or upon the prospect of opening up and developing country. We do not always insist that a railway enterprise should pay immediately, even that there should be an assurance of early profitable operation. As the hon. member for Anti-gonish and Guysborough (Mr. Mclsaac) has pointed out, here is an old settled country. I et us be reasonable in this matter. When the people in old settled districts in the Maritime provinces who for generations have not had the advantage of railway communication find that large enterprises are being undertaken in the construction of new lines in the West, it is natural that they feel that some consideration should be had for the development of that eastern country. We find no fault with the West for its ambition; we are glad to encourage the building of roads there. But if you are going to do anything to check the unrest in the eastern parts of the country you must help the construction of roads in old settled districts where for ages there has been a lack of communication That must be done if the country is to develop. This line from Sunny Brae into Guysborough county will develop an excellent agricultural district and a fine lumber district, and will touch the valuable fisheries. I think it has ultimately as fair a prospect if success as most new lines, but whether it is going to pay or not, I say it is one of the enterprises which will help to develop the Maritime provinces and I ask the committee not to be too critical as to the prospect of its paying at once.
My hon. friend means that this railway is going to be built not becau.se it will serve a useful purpose, but because it is going to please a few people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is one reason.

It is probably the chief reason; otherwise some better business reasons would be offered. The usual thing in connection with the building of railways is to have a report from an engineer on its possibilities, and I do not know why we should not have that information in this case. It rather looks to me as if the Minister of Finance was afraid of the information. What is wrong with it? It may be of course, that this board, being, apart from the president and the official connected with him, entirely a political board, do not think it necessary to have these ordinary reports. But surely it is reasonable to

C.N.R.-Construction
ask that the minister should read to the House the engineer's report as to the traffic possibilities in this case.
I did that a few moments ago; perhaps my hon. friend was not in. I read the reasons given by the board why they believed a railway line should be constructed through this territory.
I heard that. But I was asking for the report of the engineer which the board, unless, as I have said, it is purely a political board-
My hon. friend is altogether too suspicious.
I was asking for the report which would be a justification for their recommendation.
I suppose my hon. friend is making an exception of this line.
Not at all.

Perhaps with some excuse. I am going to read all that the board states in the matter; it is what their engineers, of course, have said. This memorandum reads:
The purpose of the line is to open up the local territory for lumber industry and provide better facilities for agricultural products as well as give direct communication to Guysborough for its fishing and allied products. On part of the route there is considerable agricultural development and quite extensive hardwood forests which the railway will make it possible to develop.
The original intention of the surveys for this line had in view a low grade line with the idea of making it the main line. The results of the surveys indicated that to obtain this character of line it would be very costly, and on account of the fact that the present main line could not be abandoned, and would have to be maintained and operated, it could not be shown that such a line, with its excessive cost of construction, would be justified. The present intention is to construct a line to open up the local territory and build it to cheaper standards of construction but keep in view the eventual use of it for an alternative main line or at any time this would be warranted, Therefore the line will be located so that eventually a low grade could be obtained, but employ steeper grades for the immediate construction.
It has been estimated that there are 250 million feet of hardwood and 200 million feet of softwood available to the line, and also some possibilities in gold and iron mining which have not been developed, possibly due to lack of transportation facilities.
The justification for this line is that it will serve a section of the country that has been in long need of railway communication in order to give it a real chance for development and to put the town of Guysborough in direct rail communication with the Canadian National system.

Well, that does give us some information. It says we have in sight a traffic from 250 million feet of one
kind of wood and 200 million feet of another kind. How much of that wood is being taken out now and carried by water?
I have no idea.
It was stated by the member for York-Sunbury-

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Who does not know anything about it.
Mr.GRAHAM: I am told he was altogether mistaken.
Does the engineer say that lumber operations are now carried on in that district?
I am informed that the lumber operations are not being carried on now in the district through which this road is to run.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Lumber operations are carried on now at the mouth of the St. Mary river below Sherbrooke. It is carried from there by water, but it does not touch the territory in question.

In regard to the Hanna-Medicine Hat branch in the province of Alberta, I may say that the grade south of the Red Deer river has been built for some time, but no steel has yet been laid. I see nothing in this schedule which indicates that any work is contemplated on that line. What is the board going to do with this particular piece of grade?

I can only give the same answer that I have already given to another hon. member: Out of the great number of projects submitted to the board and investigated by them, a few were selected-many were called but few were chosen. A certain number were designated as active lines; these are being proceeded with under the present programme. Others are known as inactive lines; these are projected to the extent of 584 miles at different points in the West. I could not make any promises, but I suppose there will come a time when these will have to be transferred to the active lists. At present, however, no immediate action is to be taken with regard to them. The Hanna-Medicine Hat line is in this category.

The grade south of Red Deer has been built for over three years and it is deteriorating all the time. There is just the possibility that when they do come to place steel on it they will have to do some more grading in order to bring the road-bed up to the required standard. It will be un-
C.N.R.-C onstruction

fortunate if steel is not laid this year, because the grade is going back all the time. Besides, a great deal of money would be saved if the work was proceeded with at the earliest possible moment.

The minister has sent across to me a map which shows the proposed location of the branch line to which I referred a short time ago. As I said before, I have no objection to the branch line running in the direction indicated by this map but I do want to object emphatically to the abandonment of the original route if the building of this new branch means that it will be abandoned. The Minister of Agriculture came to the defence of the new branch by stating he thought that the district was being served by a line built at right angles to the proposed line and some one hundred miles farther west. It is absolutely absurd to suggest that the building of a line at right angles to the proposed line and at such a great distance from the end of the steel could possibly serve the people in through that whole area.
There is another objection I have to make to the proposed line as shown in this schedule, and it is that it parallels and at no point appears from the survey to be seven miles away from the Canadian Pacific Railway line which is being constructed this year. It seems to me that it is not the policy that should be followed. The Canadian Pacific apparently intend to get that line through. They are building it at the present time and I can see no good service that will be done by paralleling it with the National line when there are territories which by travelling in a westerly instead of a northerly direction could be served by this lino. It is advisable perhaps to swing north for a short distance to serve the Soldier Settlement areas that I mentioned when speaking before, but it should not in my estimation go north paralleling the Canadian Pacific till it strikes the Prince Albert branch. It should turn westerly after reaching the soldier settlement areas, and then traverse the section that was originally laid out for it, and which was settled as far back as fifteen or sixteen _ years ago and has had settlers in there farming in anticipation of this line through all these years.

Is the
construction work on the Hanna-Warden line to commence this year, and is Hanna to continue to be a divisional point?

Surely hon. gentlemen do
not expect me to say where the sectional or
fMr. Gardiner.]
divisional points are going to be. That is for those in charge of the operation of the road. I might as well say who the trackmen are going to be. I cannot go into that. I have to bring before the committee certain branch lines that the Canadian National Railway Board have unanimously recommended for construction. Further than that I cannot go. The season is so far advanced that one cannot say what can be done this year. It will depend upon the conditions. Autumn will be coming soon and the men will be in the harvest fields. If we had had our appropriations through the House by early spring it would have been different, but we had not and I fear there will not be a great deal done this year.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2-Power to construct and complete lines described in schedules.
I have an amendment to move to this section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It has been moved in amendment that in section 2, after the word "completion" in the second line, the following words be inserted "-

Will the minister be good enough to give me the rate per mile which is adopted for the railways having regard to road construction as apart from the special cost? Of course he does not know where he is going to put his stations? I suppose he knows whether he has' bridging to do or not.
Some of these lines have bridges. One of them has a bridge that will cost a million and a half. You cannot compare that to any other line, because no other line might have a bridge of that kind.
That is not the point but I am glad the minister has the information as to the bridges. Perhaps he will give it.
I have given one bridge.
What is that?

Dunblane branch to
Mawer, Saskatchewan.

'That is the bridge over the Saskatchewan?

C.N.R.-Construction

Yes. With reference to some of the lines, the surveys are not definitely made, and the lines not definitely located. You cannot give the actual cost in a case of that kind. The engineers made a general estimate. My hon. friend asked me for the stations-
No, I stated that you could not tell where the stations were going to be.

Then take a short line with four stations as an example. You could give an estimate for four stations, but what is the good of asking for estimates and advertising what it is going to cost? Engineers never give out their own private data as to what things ought to cost. The engineers make an estimate, but they do not publish it. They might as well throw up their hands when they ask for tenders, if they are going to announce what they think the work ought to cost.
Taking the very first one, Slot),000, is that an estimate of what it ought to cost?
Yes that is everything complete on the line.
Everything is covered in the $150,000 in connection with the first item.
That includes everything.
Suppose we take them all, so as to save time; do these figures include the cost necessary in order to have these lines built and ready for operation?
Yes, so far as it is humanly possible to estimate what the cost will be. This is to complete the line.
So that all the work is covered. Whose estimates of cost are these ?
They are prepared by the engineers in the locality, and passed on to the chief engineer at the head office.
And checked by the chief engineer?
Yes.

I would like to ask the
minister some questions in regard to what is generally known as the Oliver-St. Paul railway. That is the railway running from Edmonton to North Battleford. It is completed as far as St. Paul. It runs from the east as far as St. Walburg, leaving a gap of about eighty
miles. This railway has been promised the people in that vicinity for some fourteen years. The country is well settled. It is a very good country, but it is particularly handicapped, because to the south runs the Saskatchewan river, across which there are no bridges in the particular part to which I am referring, and they have to use ferries. At the present time the railway has a double haul on all produce being taken to St. Paul, which would bring the extra distance to about 300 miles, taking the run to Edmonton and back again via Vermilion. It seems to me it would be in the best interests of the country if that gap were completed. I see in the schedule under item 25 it is only proposed to build the railway to a point twenty-one miles east of St. Paul. As this is a three-year programme, would the minister kindly give me the reason why the plans were not made to carry it further than mile 21? I will have more questions to ask later.

This is for hon. members whose lines are not taken in the programme but not so much for those whose lines are partially taken in. The same answer is applicable to all the requests of members in whose constituency no extensions are being made. This is all the Canadian National Board thought it wise at present to include in the programme. Every one will realize that the financial condition of the country will not allow us to launch out into what might be useful enterprises. We have to go along very slowly, to show our good intentions, but hope the conditions will continue to improve until all our hopes are realized in the development of the country and the development of the railways as well.

I appreciate very much
what is being done, but if there is no guarantee of some sort that work is going to be continued for probably several years to complete the line from St. Paul to St. Walburg, we will not be able to keep the settlers in that country. The settlers have been there for a good many years. They are hauling in some instances upwards of 100 miles and if they have not some sort of guarantee that the gap will be completed, I am very much afraid we will lose a great many of- them. I would ask the minister if we can look for the completion of that line within the three-year limit?

I should like to corroborate what the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) has said regarding this line. I do not intend to add to what he said, in order to save the time of the committee. Is it the
C.N.R.-C tinstruction

intention of the Board of Directors of the Canadian National Railways to change the location of the line, the construction of which is necessary to fill that gap? I understand a more northerly route has been surveyed?

Would that appertain to
the northern route or the southern route?

The southern route is the expensive one. Another and bill investigation is going to be made of the proposed route or routes before a final decision is reached During the winter a very strong deputation waited on me with all the information. They impressed me, but I do not know anything about the practical construction. The question, however, will be fully considered, and what is thought best in the interest of the whole country will be decided upon.

I wish to refer the Minister of Railways to certain evidence which was brought out during the present session before the committee on Mines and Minerals. This evidence showed the grave necessity, if we wish to develop our coal industry, of extending and building certain lines of railways. I understand my colleague from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) this afternoon directed the attention of the minister to the necessity of extending the Point Tupper-St. Peters road into the town of Louis-burg.
How many miles?

Sixty miles. According to the evidence which was brought out before our committee, that proposition would develop a very large number of mines in the vicinity. Then there should be the extension, if the government takes over the road, of the Inverness and Richmond railway, which now runs from Port Ilawkesbury to Point Tupper, to the town of Inverness. In the committee there was also a proposition for a railway in the Peace river district to connect with the Grand Trunk railway. This line would develop

a trade between that country and the Pacific coast. I am not interested locally in that matter, but I think the minister might find it worth his time to read over the evidence given by western gentlemen before that committee in connection with that line. He might also find it worth his while to read the evidence of eastern gentlemen before that committee as to the necessity of extending and building those eastern lines. We in this country, I hope, are attempting to arouse me people, governments, coal operators, transportation agencies, to the necessity of having a national fuel supply for Canada. Those gentlemen have come to Ottawa and have developed those ideas which I am suggesting to the minister, and I do not think I could make the cases any stronger for those roais than did those witnesses who under oath gave evidence in connection with those matters. While this year I am not asking for the extension or building of these lines, the reason why I personally am not doing so, is because I understood the government was not going into new operations of this kind. If I had so understood, I would have been after the minister day and night in connection with the matter. I do not think I can make the case any stronger for those three roads, than the gentlemen who gave evidence.
What are the three roads?

The extension of the line from St. Peters to Louisburg; the extension of the Richmond-Inverness road to Inverness, a distance of 18 or 20 miles, which would develop and open up one of the great resources of coal in this country. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) probably would mention the road in the western country, concerning which road much evidence was given before our fuel committee. Those are the three roads. I would respectfully suggest to the minister that when he has some spare time, he might, perhaps, read over the evidence given in connection with those roads. This evidence given before the committee on Mines and Minerals will be laid on the Table to-morrow or the day after. If he does,
I am sure next year, without any exhortation on the part of any one in this House, he will be glad to bring down legislation for the construction and the extension of the lines I have mentioned.

I realize the limitations that are placed upon the government in regard to the matter of spending money to provide the many branch lines of railways which have been asked for, but I think my case has precedence over a goodly number. I have thought

C.AT.R.-Construction
that the last government attempted to do penance, in that the road had been promised a long time ago, and they had even had graded some 16 or 18 miles. The farmers living along that grade did most of the work in their anxiety to have the road built. I speak of No. 9, the road from Peebles to Lampman. In my humble opinion, the road was commenced at the wrong end, simply because, had it started from the town of Lampman, it would have connected with the branch line to Bienfait and the coal fields north of the town of Lampman about 9 miles. That is a very urgent question in our part of the country, in that we are deprived of an adequate supply of fuel. The road likewise would have terminated on our own lines of railway, and this would have given an opportunity to cur farmers to get their grain out. At the present time, all the grain in that territory is drawn to the lines of the Canadian Pacific. The road starts at Peebles in the district of Qu'-Appelle, represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Millar), and it comes into the district of Assiniboia about 6 miles, coming down the west side of the Moose mountains. There is a very high, mountainous country to the east of the road. If the road had been continued another 7 or 8 miles, even while it would not have tapped the coal fields, it would have facilitated the getting of grain to this railway much better than at the present time.	.
A further thing I wish to say in connection with this matter, is that materials, ties and steel, had been brought along the graded road in quantities sufficient, I think, to grade 11 miles, and last year the larger part of that material was removed. I cite this as an argument why we should have more consideration, if further consideration is to be given. I know the people living south of the present line of road will feel quite keenly disappointed,, in that the survey had been through there for a number of years to the town of Lampman, and provision is not made in the bill to carry the road further than Mile 22. I think that under this programme it should really go another 7 or 8 miles, or a total of 30 miles, to Lampman. In that way it would give direct access from our own line of railways to the coal fields. I am not urging this on the minister, and I am thankful that provision is made for the 22 miles. But if opportunity offers in the very near future, to extend this line further, I trust due consideration will be given to the matter.

My hon. friend has not said what he is going to do for us in
Toronto, in connection with the tremendous deadlock that we have at the union station there. We had a long and eloquent speech which I enjoyed very much, but I should have appreciated it to a greater extent had I been able to understand completely why emphasis should be laid upon the construction of more railways in Quebec in preference to the carrying out of work in other parts of the country. As I understood the hon. gentleman, he wanted more work done in Quebec, and he pointed out in very beautiful language the advantages of the country through which the railways would run. He showed how much more important it was to have done what he was advocating than it was to do the little work in Toronto to which I referred this afternoon. He declared that little was done for the province of Quebec. I do not ask that anything be done especially for one part of the country as against another; I do not think that we have any right to consider at all whether any work is to be carried out in Ontario, in Quebec, in Manitoba, or anywhere else. The whole question should be whether it is right that such work be gone on with. The statement was made that it was very much more important to look after this new line of railway in Quebec than to right what is a flagrant wrong which has been going on for some time and is getting worse all the time. If we are to discuss this question of the relative importance of various works in different parts of the country, I would point out to the committee that the system that is making money down in this section of the Dominion, the Grand Trunk system, earned in Ontario $26,000,000 largely through that very terminal business in Toronto, as against the sum of slightly over $5,000,000 in the province of Quebec. It is utterly idle for people to try to make these comparisons: As I say, the whole question in regard to expenditures that are to be made anywhere should be as to whether or not those expenditures are justifiable. Surely my hon. friend should indicate to the committee where we shall land if we neglect the matter to which I referred this afternoon and of which I am speaking now. Surely he does not want the municipality to spend more money. It is out $26,000,000 now, and I cannot believe that the hon. gentleman would want to subject it to further inconvenience and harass it any longer. The people of Toronto have been menaced too long now. Thousands, yes sometimes eighty thousand, ninety thousand, and even a hundred thousand people using the crossings have been held up in one day, often in imminent peril. Does the hon. gentleman want that condition of affairs to continue and to be aggravated? I am sure
C.N.R.-Construction

that the board must have some policy by this time in connection with this matter, and the serious complaint of central Toronto demands by way of answer more than mere silence on the part of the minister.

My hon. friend was not here this afternoon. It will have to continue until parliament decides to issue securities against the government-owned railways. Personally, I do not think that would be a good idea to-day.

Does it not really turn on whether you think it is a good idea to work these absolutely into one property or not? If we are to have two sets of accounts -and apparently we are-it is costing just so much more money. Is it not a good deal better for the government to show what the property is charged so the net debt will not look any worse than it really is? I cannot see anything in the objection. Of course if the idea is that the whole system is to be kept so that it can be unscrambled at any time, and in the meantime we are to have merely temporary joint management instead of one hundred per cent co-ordination with one hundred per cent economy, it is all right.

I would not think that. There is a strong feeling against bringing the old government-owned lines under a mortgage which they have never yet carried. I think separate accounts will have to be kept. The capital account of the government railways is simple, but I admit there is difficulty'in keeping the accounts separate as between the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, a difficulty which we are trying to eliminate. It costs a lot of money, it is true, but in this respect I think it is not expensive.

Apparently there is nothing but a sentimental objection to having the mortgage that we really owe cover our own lines. All the government need do is simply to convey the government-owned lines to the Canadian National Railway system. This would be merely a conveyance of the fee simple. Once this is done, instead of continuing about five different systems of book-keeping one should be sufficient. I do not doubt at all that it would save the country-well, close to a million dollars a year.

I still think that for the
present at least the better way is to leave it as it is. It does not cost a considerable amount to keep the separate accounts. For example, the accounts of the Grand Trunk and the Grank Trunk Pacific have to be kept separate because the interest on the Grand Trunk Pacific guaranteed debenture stock is payable contingent upon the earnings of the old Grand Trunk, and you have to keep the accounts of the Grand Trunk separate for that purpose. We are trying to unscramble

it, as my hon. friend says, but it is not so easy.

That is true; you have
to keep the accounts separate in order to be able to determine whether the Grand Trunk has sufficient earnings to meet the interest on all these Grand Trunk Pacific debentures, and the same applies to the Canadian Northern income convertible bonds. Well, I suggest that at the earliest possible day the government make some sort of settlement with both. I think it would pay if the settlement were arrived at in a proper way and on a very modest basis to get rid of all this necessity for separate systems and separate book-keeping. But I hope the [DOT] government will have the matter fully discussed here before they do that; I do not like to trust them to make any outside deal. Perhaps, while I am on my feet, I might ask how that syndicate is getting along in New York. Have the names got to the surface yet? Are they still on Fifth avenue?
I have not seen the names yet.
Is the minister yet able to produce that lawyer's letter guaranteeing the legality of the transaction? I would like, I think, to suggest that a reward be offered for the production of that letter.

As the subject is sure to come up again, I here and now challenge the minister to get any lawyer in the employ of the Canadian National Railway Company, to recite what this company has done in connection with that hotel and say it is legal.

Canadian National Railways are not of necessity government railways; they are owned by a company. My idea is that every branch line that connects with and becomes a part of the Canadian Government Railways, strictly speaking, might well be called a branch of the government railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not enough.

Of course it is enough; the minister will find it is plenty if he will think the matter over. Take the case of tfie Merchant Marine. We did not specify the boats in the statute; we passed a vote to enable them to be built and then laid before parliament all the facts connected with their construction. This is money voted for the railways for such purposes as parliament has intimation of in a statement submitted to parliament. Where was the bill before about extensions? I have no recollection of it. Can the minister tell me? These were covered in the regular vote. Now then what the government is seeking to do, and I warn the House in time, is to be able to show a difference through this vote between the total estimate for the year and the previous year, and at the same time be spending the money under cover of another bill without its appearing in the Estimates. That is the effect of it all. In the past the votes have appeared. The country has known when the budget for the year was presented to the nation what it was going to be committed to for the ensuing year. But if this policy i3 followed it is not going to know. It is true that in a case like the agricultural education grant where a certain definite amount and n / more was granted each year for a certain period, ten years I think, towards agricultural education, that was a statutory vote and so much per year was paid out, but there was no previous system of doing it otherwise in that case as there has been for this. Furthermore the country knew each year from the statutes what its commitment was, but he*e

we do not know what our commitment is for any year. This government is simpij' asking for a blank cheque to be spent at any hour of any day within the next three years and avoiding putting an amount in the Estimates any year. Now that is something new. In fact, there is scarcely ever a statute this government submits to parliament that has not concealed in it an attempt to draw more power all the time into the administration-more of this order in council authority. This is definitely and irrefutably an attempt of that kind.
Now what I ask the government to do is this: If you want to go ahead with a special act, all right, but put in that special act the usual clause that the money for the purpose shall be voted by the Commons of this country. Then we shall know just exactly what we are doing and what the money is going to be applied to. I raised this point on the main motion and I intend to press it now. The government should not ask for a blank cheque covering three years when the country does not know how much is going to be spent in any year at all. It should not ask for power to spend this money at any time and at whatever time it suits the governmeit best, whatever time it suits the exigencies best. Let the government add a clause here that the Appropriation Act that covered it in the past shall cover it in the future.

9 p.m. case of the agricultural education grant. I have not looked up subsidies and I am not going to say yes or no whether it was done in that case or not. No. They had of course to pass the order in council, but the railway was entitled to the subsidy if it went ahead, and it could wait ten or fifteen years. There was reason in that case. But here the government knows, or should know, because we own the stock, what they are going on with and what they are are not going on with, and there is no reason why they should not show in the Estimates just what they are going to spend. Why is this done? What is going to be spent? What is the reason for taking
it out of the Estimates? The reason is clear to my mind. The government wants to be able to draw an unfair and unjust comparison of its Estimates this year and in future years with those of previous years.

My hon. friend will be
here to see that that is not permitted, and I know he will do it well; he always does.

That is all right, but
when the minister gets before the country he will hold up the Estimates, and I cannot follow him through the country or even through the papers.

I will take him with me
next time, and as for my paper it has been mighty decent to him at a time when he needed it. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has explained fully to the committee why this is necessary. He spoke of subsidies. Now the reason why that method might have been necessary was because the government did not know how many miles would be constructed in any year, and that is the answer here to a large extent. The Canadian National Railway Board is going to construct these lines. This season they cannot construct much, but next year on account of this act, through not having to wait for construction to begin until after the estimates are through, construction can begin early in the season and be continued right along. The board know what they can do and how much they can construct, but if they have to wait year after year until the Estimates are through before they can start construction, experience shows that that is impracticable. The construction of these railways ought to be rushed wherever they are being constructed at times when labour can be secured between busy seasons. If we have to wait every year until the estimates are through construction will be held off for three months. The financial year ends March 31 and there would be no more money to go on with construction until the last estimates were through the House. Hon. gentlemen know that the men who would wish to get on this construction work during the summer would probably be needed on the farms later on in the year for harvesting. It is very difficult to get labour at such times.
There is no endeavour to hide anything here. It is simply to place a three years' programme and vote the money so that we shall not have to wait every year until the estimates are through before we can start construction. If this work were all going to be completed this year, it would be a different

matter. We could say we are going to need this much, and clean it up, but we do not pretend that all this construction will be completed this year. The programme is for three years, and there is no attempt whatever at deception. Under the old estimates there were certain small extensions and so on, and my hon. friend will appreciate the difficulties under that method. He graded 372 miles, yes, 500 miles, in the West and then stopped. Now under a three years' programme at least some of these lines would have been completed in the three years, but as it was they were not. Many of these lines have rails on them; they are graded now, but the grade in some places is partially destroyed, I suppose. To my mind it is merely a matter of horse sense to proceed by this method. Let the company know for three years what they can depend on. Here are the amounts and it is no trouble to keep track of them. Parliament will have full opportunity to discuss them. I think this is the absolute business way to carry on this project.

My hon. friend has cleared up the situation rather well. He has put it so we can understand it, at any rate. It is a change, just as my hon. leader said. It is a complete change from what was done before. It makes a complete change in the basis of the estimate. He points out that of course this was not done before. We had it from the Minister of Finance that it was done before-no change at all. Of course there is a change and of course all this capital construction was controlled and voted by the House. There is no doubt about it and the minister makes it clear. Now, he says there is an objection to that and that is that you cannot spend all your money in the one year. If it is a good objection that you cannot spend all your money in the one year, there is no reason why parliament should ever look after the estimates at all. There is hardly an estimate of any size in which there is not that item of revote. Every department has its revote. Is that any reason why some irresponsible commission should have the right of looking after the whole thing without coming back to parliament? Is that any reason why the departmental estimates should not still be submitted? But there is the whole thing: You do not know how much you are going to spend, and, therefore, you should not do it by way of estimates! You do not know how much you are going to add this year or next. The whole truth is that there is just one thing that is of any importance here, and I have not been able to get it. If we can have definite estimates of such a character

laid on the Table that we know that the whole work is going to be done under the one vote, without coming back again, it will be a good thing. I could not get anything definite today-not a thing. There is absolutely no guarantee to the House in connection with it.
Was there ever in connection with any public work?

I am saying that is the only thing that is of any use, if you can get it in connection with the three-year lease, so that you will not have the officials coming back time after time with the larger votes. We have not anything more definite here than we have in connection with the building of a $500 post office. We have practically no details at all in connection with the $28,000,000 programme. My hon. friend says we have rights of way and dumps and all that sort of thing and that we did not go on with them. That did not make a bit of difference as to any three years' business-not the slightest. It was the inescapable condition that we and the country were in. That was all and nothing else. The mere fact of a bill would not have produced any money, and the mere fact of this bill will not produce any money. The country might just as well understand that this is a complete change from the former method of accounting under which, in connection with the railway estimates each year, the country knew just exactly what their railways were costing for everything. But the whole commitment, whether on capital account, construction account, guarantee or deficit, was all there. Now the country wants to know about it. There is nothing in the bill to say the return is to be made from the commencement, showing how many miles have been constructed, and where, and showing how much money has been expended. Has the minister taken any precaution in connection with these votes to prevent switching of public funds from one purpose to another? What guarantee have we, for example, that when we vote $3,000,000 for the purpose of a railway that the money is going to be spent there and not somewhere else-that the money, perhaps, is not going to be spent in Germany next time, instead of in France, as the other vote was spent?

I think the auditors should be depended on to look after that. They are more competent to deal with that phase than I am. As to everything being in the Estimates, I can point out to my hon. friend that refunding of the Canadian Northern was provided for under the statute and not under the Estimates.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that the Canadian National Railways have taken in the Canadian Northern, along with the Halifax and Southwestern road, and I would like to ask whether or not the present government has considered the advisability of constructing a railway from Windsor in Hants county to a point at or near Chester in the county of Lunenburg? This has been a political question for years and has been made a poli-cal foptball by every party in this country. A railway from Windsor in Hants county to a point at or near Chester in the county of Lunenburg would pass through Martock, Windsor Forks, Leminster or Chester Road, a magnificent lumbering country, and would supply a great deal of wood for shipment over the Halifax and Southwestern which is now owned by the government. I am not going to enter into a discussion of the merits of the question, but I would like an assurance from the minister that he will have Sir Henry Thornton look into the advisability of proceeding with this branch, because it would be a very valuable line for the people in that section of the country. It is particularly necessary to have the question looked into, now that the government owns the Halifax and Southwestern, and I would like to have a promise from the minister.
I shall note the remarks my hon. friend has made and place them before Sir Henry Thornton.
I have more confidence in the minister than in Sir Henry Thornton.

I do not know whether there can be said to be any political advantage in providing for a bill of this description. If, as we understand, the Canadian National Railways are outside of politics, then I understand that the schedule has been presented by the National Railway to parliament to vote this amount of money, and if parliament votes this amount of money for three years, it seems to me that no party will be able to go out in the ridings and claim any political advantage. If I understood the minister aright as to how this sum is voted, there is only one way in which it can be spent, and that is on the particular lines which have been indicated in the bill.
I wish to say a few words in regard to item No. 19-Dunblane branch. I had an opportunity of speaking to the minister and those in charge before recess, and I have the arguments in regard to the matter. Yet, at the same time I have received a great many telegrams from county councillors and also farmers in the vicinity, against the expenditure of this money in the particular way in which it is proposed to spend it. There is one thing to be considered as regards this branch line that proceeds from Moose Jaw to Riverhuret. It was generally understood by the people in that vicinity that at some time or another the line to River-hurst would be extended beyond the river to link up with some of the other National lines. With that result in view, Riverhurst has become an important town. In 1921, a large sum of money was spent near Riverhurst in providing for a dam for a splendid water supply for the town and for the railway to Moose Jaw. Furthermore, Riverhurst is a divisional point. If this proposed railway is constructed, Riverhurst will become simply a dead end so far as we are able to understand the matter. I do not think there is any agitation at present from the people in the vicinity for the line to take the route which it is proposed it should take. As regards the railway situation, I know the whole country like a book, and the two railways, the Canadian Pacific to Elbow and the Grand Trunk to Riverhurst practically run parallel. There is no place where they are 20 miles apart. On the Canadian Pacific side for the last 15 to 20 miles, the country is simply sand hills, and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) a short time ago brought down a bill whereby the people in that district had the right to relinquish their lands, to give them back to
C.N.R.-C <-instruction

the government and to receive lands in territory where they might be able to farm. After this railway proceeds a few miles north of Lawson and then in a northwesterly direction to Elbow, I do not think for 15 miles it will pass a single inhabited house. A person taking an automobile ride from, say, Lawson, north to Elbow, where this railway is about to run, after proceeding 6 miles north, would for the next 10 miles, hardly see a dwelling house for the simple reason that the northwesterly winds sweeping over the sand hills have covered even the good lands with sand, with the result that the people have gone to more fertile fields to farm. I understand from the engineers' report that this line is taking this particular direction, on account of the easier grade. It will be an easier grade for the railway, and it will be able to link up with the system across the river. The line, however, will not be any shorter. It will certainly mean, at last, building a line 30 miles longer than they would have to build if they continued the present line. The people south of the railway line have always expected that this line some day would be completed and would cross the river at Lucky lake and be linked up with that system. I can readily understand, if the railway which is contemplated in the bill ever is constructed, the government will never see fit to build another railway bridge, at least 20 miles south, with the result that the people on the fertile land south of the Grand Trunk will have to depend simply on a tri-weekly service, where on the other hand, if it is linked up to Dunblane with a line across the Saskatchewan river, they will have the advantage of the good service; but there will be no service for the railway to perform so far as that particular stretch of line is concerned.
I understand from the report that no part of this line will be built this year; that it will be proceeded with next year. I do not wish to stop this expenditure, nor to make any protest as to this item going through; but if the money must be spent in the particular way in which the minister states, it would be wise to hold the matter over until an investigation is made. Surely the engineers who built the railway in the first place from Moose Jaw to Riverhurst never intended that River-hurst should become a dead end. They had something in view, or they would never have built 80 miles of line, made a divisional point at the far end, and then built a splendid dam costing thousands of dollars, with the intention of that town becoming a dead end. They intended to cross the river somewhere in the 
vicinity of Riverhurst, and to link it up with the line across the river. This proposed line will run through a territory that is not even calling for the line west and north to Elbow, and it crosses the same Saskatchewan river. It is true on the east side of the Saskatchewan river there is no great bank difficulty to overcome; but when you come to the other side, in order to reach Dunblane, you have to have a bridge that will be high enough to surmount the hill which is hundreds of feet high, and at the same time the line must pass through a very sandy territory to get there. It seems to me the pledge to the people living in the good territory who are producing wheat and making the railway pay, should be carried out, and they should have an opportunity of seeing the line extended across the river into the same kind of territory where the same service will be rendered to the same people, and where the line at the same time will cost a good deal less. I understand there is a report on the situation, and before I can speak definitely and intelligently on it, I should like to hear the minister's report as regards this particular line. I hope he will again look into the matter, and although I do not think we have any right to interfere with the policy of the National Railways, yet due consideration should be given to the people who are living in that territory and to the pledges that were made to them some years ago when they went into that territory and also formed a town.

According to my hon.
friend the farm furthest from the stub, end would be only 12 miles?
Yes.

That would be the furthest farmer away at that end. I do not blame my hon. friend for putting in a strong plea for those people. They are pretty well served now. But in order to make a through connection between the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, to get a through line with good grades from Regina to Moose Jaw, the engineers say that it is necessary to build this other line in the manner proposed. It is through traffic they are after with the best grades possible. The best grade it is possible to get on the line proposed by my hon. friend is a full one per cent. In the other case, they can easily get a grade of one-half of one per cent. This makes a great difference in the load that can be hauled on through traffic and on the cost of transportation. If it be true, as it is, that the lower the grade, the cheaper the transportation,

C.N.R.-Construction
surely it is in the interest of the farmers themselves, who are not too far away from the railway as none of them are, that they should have the best standard of railway that can be constructed for the through traffic. In addition to that, the cost of those 42 miles to the bridge, I am told, will be little if any more than the cost of the 12 miles with the bridge at the point where that road would cross the river.

As regards the question where the bridge is going to be placed, I should like to make a suggestion. So far as I know at present, there is no possible way of getting across the Saskatchewan river. This government owns the resources of the province of Saskatchewan. I understand the rivers are also under federal jurisdiction, so at present the only way in which the people have a chance of getting across the Saskatchewan river, which is a very deadly river, is by a ferry. I hope when such a bridge is contemplated, not only will they contemplate a bridge for trains, but they will consider an additional expense whereby a traffic bridge can be built. At the present time one would have to go right to Saskatoon, one hundred miles north, before one could find a bridge for traffic to cross the river.
I do not wish to say anything derogatory about the engineers, but let us consider just for a moment the methods of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That line starts from Moose Jaw and goes up to Elbow, in identically the same locality the government intends to run its railway. At Elbow on the Saskatchewan river the Canadian Pacific Railway decided that the crossing was not a good one and so it goes immediately north about thirty miles before it crosses the Saskatchewan river. Now if the Canadian Pacific Railway thinks rhat Elbow is not a convenient place at which to cross and its engineers find it necessary to go straight north thirty miles to Outlook before crossing the Saskatchewan river, it does seem rather strange that another set of engineers should come along a little time afterwards and decide that the crossing which the Canadian Pacific engineers considered undesirable is good enough for the Canadian National Railways. I say it does strike me at least as somewhat peculiar. But wherever the bridge is built I trust that traffic accommodation will be provided and that the people will have the fullest opportunity of crossing the river.
That will be a question between the railway company and the provincial authorities.
I hope it will be taken into serious consideration.

I was alarmed a few minutes ago when I heard the minister state that in connection with branch lines not much could be done this year. I do not know whether I understood him rightly or not, but that is what I gathered at any rate. And the more am I alarmed when I realize how near we are to the first of July and how short a part of the season is left. Is it the intention of the government to do very little on the branch lines this year? If so, and very little can be done because of the shortness of the season, why could this matter not have been brought down several weeks ago? We have been passing estimates now for nearly two months and I do not see why this matter could not have been attended to before now. I can assure the minister that there will be the most bitter disappointment in the country with regard to item No. 9 if the proposed line is not dealt with this year. This is a district that is well settled. It has been settled now for fifteen or twenty years and the people are obliged to haul their produce seventeen, eighteen and nineteen miles over roads that are not like the Ontario roads by any means. Can the minister imagine what it must mean to haul grain that distance over mud roads? Not only that, but most of the grain is now going to the Canadian Pacific Railway, whereas if this branch line were built it would go by the Canadian National. I am sure that the people of this district will be very grateful to the government for undertaking to build this line even in the next three years, but at the same time they will resent the injustice of postponing it even beyond this year. The road has been graded for some time and the ties are waiting to be laid down; and very little more expenditure would have been necessary to complete the work, so that the settlers could have taken their grain out this fall. I shall be sorry if anything is done to delay the work and prevent this line being built until next year.

My hon. friend can
realize the difficulty in this matter. Every hon. gentleman feels that his particular case is the most urgent and there are about ten times as many interested parties outside who have to be heard. All this must be considered and sifted and resifted and it is not easy

to select from so many when there is such a diversity of representation. The company hopes to conclude the line to which my hon. friend refers this year.

I would draw
the minister's attention to item 26, which is a joint section with the Canadian Pacific Railway. There are millions of dollars to be voted for the expansion of our railway system in competition with the Canadian Pacific. We are entering on a period of rival construction between the two great systems. Probably a question of absorbing interest to the people to-day is whether there is to be a policy of rival construction between the two roads with the resultant waste of money and lack of efficiency of service which co-operation and co-ordination would avoid. It is time that we scrutinized all these votes to see whether they are for lines to compete with existing lines, in whcb case the money might better be devoted to provide railway facilities in those portions of the country which require them. I would ask the minister if a policy has been decided upon between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway so that instead of blind competition in the building of roads where they are not needed there will be co-operation to serve the best interests of the people at large. We should not conclude this session without making a declaration in regard to this matter. It is not only up to the government but up to the administration of the National Railways and the Canadian Pacific to say whether they intend to embark on a policy of rival construction. We want efficient construction in this country, not mad rivalry. I should like to hear from the minister on this point.

That is largely something to be worked out between the railways. I think the day for mad rivalry is over in the interests of economy. As an object lesson, there are a couple of items in this schedule where two railways are running over the same track for a certain distance.

The truth is that someone is determined that the whole of this matter is to be left up in the. air for somebody to handle just in the way somebody wants to handle it. When the minister gets an omnibus power like this, how is he going to see that the public funds are not switched from one purpose to another? I indicate to him whal happened in the case of the Hotel Scribe, and he says the auditors can look after it. We are now coming to the sections which put in concrete form just what we have been saying. We have on the one hand the guarantees to be given under this act, and on the other hand the guarantees given under the vote already made by this House. Now I ask my hon. friend what portion of the main vote is for a similar purpose to what we have here.
I can inform my hon. friend that there is nothing in the $73,000,000 vote passed this year except for betterments and co-ordination between the various lines. There was nothing for building.

If it is, it is different to any other vote we have had. It may have been prepared with that end in view. I would go further and say that if there is no construction whatever contemplated in the vote this year of $73,000,000 it is a bigger vote than we had last year. I asked my hon. friend for full particulars as to that vote. I did get a subdivision from him, and the day I got it I wrote to him pointing out that it was not at all full and did not give definite details as to what we were voting. I wonder if he has any objection to giving now the information asked for, or whether the information is to be withheld from parliament.

We prepared what we understood my hon. friend wanted and we gave that to him. Further details are being prepared, but it will take some little time to get that done. My hon. friend knows that in the operation and management of any big railway system the estimates presented to the board of railway directors are not inflexible in their application, because the directors could not meet any exigency if they were unable to make any change from their first plans. I think my hon. friend will find if he looks into the operation and management and even the betterments of any of the great railway systems that while generally they have to proceed along certain lines, exigencies might arise which might make a difference altogether in the original plans, and if the appropriation were inflexible the management would be practically precluded from operating successfully. I do not mean that they should be wide open but there must be a certain amount of flexibility, particularly in the operation and management and even in the betterments of a railway.

I think my hon. friend knows perfectly well what I want. How the situation looks to me at present, and I indicated it at a previous sitting of ths House; is this: We have got a vote within $4,000,000 of the whole vote of last year. We had a deficit running into several million dollars, and now according to the statement my hon. friend made to the House, and I suppose the statement is true, and I want to continue thinking the statement is true, he showed that instead of that deficit he had a surplus of $4,000,000; but notwithstanding that

surplus of $4,000,000 and notwithstanding the fact that the estimates this year, as we have been told, do not include five cents for construction there is only a difference of $4,000,000 between the vote this year and last. My hon. friend talks about elasticity. I think there has been a great deal too much elasticity. I believe if there had not been such a lot of elasticity the amount used could not have been used. My hon. friend asks me what was done. I know that we have had pages and pages of details giving us information as to the estimates to be voted before they were brought down to the House, and my hon. friend must have those details. If the work is being carried on in the way it used to be, the minister and the department is given full information as to the commitments here, there and everywhere. Why, it is a matter of hours going through those details, and if the proper details have been given my hon. friend for the purposes of this vote there is no difficulty in him giving that information to the House. He can table the information now in two minutes because he has it.

Would -my hon. friend
table all the details of notes he had from his
department?
Certainly I would give the details.
He never did, and that information was never asked for before.

I would certainly detail every bit of information I had leading to an estimate. My hon. friend has those details and he has not given me the information. Now we might just as well know where we are about it. The department have the details and there is only one reason for not giving them, and that reason is that moneys that are voted for this purpose can be applied to that. That is just what my hon. friend calls elasticity, and that is just what is absolutely wrong.

There is not one iota of change this year from last year or any other year. My hon. friend from his own intimate knowledge knows that there are a lot of things he never gave to the House and a lot of things that nobody ever asks for in the House. I say quite candidly I would have notes. He did himself many a time have notes from his subordinates, but he would not lay them on the Table. They are notes of particular information for the minister. My hon. friend has asked me questions by the score to-day that never were asked before in this House

by any other member. In his time he never pretended to give any such information to the House. I have been a member of the House as long as he has, and I have put through some railway estimates in my time, more than he ever did, and never in my time were the details that were given to the minister in his book in order to answer questions, placed on the Table of the House or asked 10 p.m. to be placed on the Table of the House. There are many things in that book that are not public property. There are many things in it for the information of the minister alone, and my hon. friend knows that.
Now as to showing a surplus, that was not to glorify the present government or the National Railway Board, because that was the result of the work of my hon. friend's board except from the month of October. If we had wished to minimize what they had done we could have made it appear very bad last year and make it look good this year, but we gave an honest statement of what had occurred, and it was to the credit of the board headed by Mr. Hanna. The credit was not taken for this by the government or the government's board. I tried to get every possible bit of information. I said we were endeavouring to make another statement. We sent my hon. friend one. I thought, and my deputy thought, it covered everything. Now he asks that we place on the Table of the House private information,-I say semi-private information-some of it absolutely public, given to the minister in order to answer every question, right or wrong, incidental or otherwise that might be asked, and he asks that that be placed on the Table of the House-something never heard of in the world before.

My hon. friend
knows very well that the answer is not at all in line with the argument I made. I made no complaint whatever about the surplus being discussed.

They are entirely different, and I ask, when did we refuse to give any information asked for, having regard to an estimate before the House?

I have never said my
hon. friend did. I have said it was absolutely contrary to practice to ask the minister to place his book of information given to him on various matters on the Table of the House. I wish to ask the minister a question. I know that this point has been discussed to-night on a previous section, but I think my question is pertinent and ought to be clearly answered, particularly
