in face of the corhments made a moment ago by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). Section 8 which is now before the committee empowers the issue of certain securities in a manner which shall be determined by the Governor in Council from time to time, and then it goes on to provide that these securities may be secured by a mortgage or deed of trust, and so forth. From that it would appear that this particular expenditure of some twenty or twenty-five million dollars is to be made in an issue of new securities distinct from those provided for in the issue. What I want to ask the minister is this: Why is it necessary, in connection. with this work set forth in the schedule to this bill, to authorize this issue of new securities when, in the estimates we provide for the sum of $73,000,000 in connection with which I read this in subsection (e), of the description:
Construction and betterments: guarantee of securities.
And then it says:
If by way of guarantee, any such guarantee may De of the principal and interest of the notes and obligations or securities of one or more such companies specified by the Governor in Council.
And so forth.
In other words, in the estimates out of the $73,000,000 we are providing for the issue and guarantee of securities for construction, for extension, principal and interest of maturing and matured loans, and so forth. Yet for this particular schedule of branch lines we are making a separate issue of securities which will not appear in the ordinary statements of the government next year, or as an increase, for instance, in the public debt. It will not appear in any definite form. In the past

that is last year and the year before-we had these votes and the public were told that the National Railways had a deficit of a certain amount. Then this amount was segregated into losses on operation, refunding and so forth. These particular works provided for in this bill are not distinct and separate from works being carried on under the Main Estimates. I am quite aware that the minister may reply that this is capital expenditure; as a matter of fact, we have provided in the $73,000,000 item for what is just as clearly capital expenditure as is this item in this bill. I do not wish to weary the committee by asking for information that, perhaps, has been given already. Yet I have failed to see the need of this being done in this particular form, especially since the minister has refused to make provision in the estimates. I would have no particular ob-

jection to this bill, if the actual expenditure of the money to provide for the work were contained in the estimates from year to year, but that has been decided in clauses 4 and 7. The minister has refused to include those in the estimates, and he makes the provision in this form. I should like the minister to explain why we have capital expenditures in the main Estimates, and this item appearing in a different form in the bill.
I imagine it would not be satisfactory to parliament if, under the appropriation that we have, we launched out on a great construction scheme such as this.
No.

Any work that was done under the powers of a guarantee, or issuing of securities, or estimates is work in connection with co-ordination, minor work, betterments and all that kind of thing, no large construction of the dimensions of this. For practical purposes it is thought better to take this special construction in this way, and I believe parliament will find this the better way. As regards information, the Minister of Railways in the annual statement that he makes before coming to parliament with his ordinary estimates, will be compelled to give in _ detail what has been done during the year in this connection, and the public accounts committee will have an opportunity of going into the matter. This railway system amounting to 22,600 miles is a new thing, and we have to do these big things in a somewhat different way from what we did when we had just the Intercolonial. This system is many thousands of miles longer than it was a year ago. This method is only for practicability, there is nothing whatever to be hidden, and I do not think my hon. friend believes that anything is to be hidden. Everything possible will be given in the minister's statement, which, I believe, will be the proper place in which to give the information.

These items in the estimates to which I have referred, will all appear in the public accounts, and will be placed before parliament at the end of the year. These items in the bill will not necessarily be included in the public accounts unless in some form, possibly as a supplement. That might be done, but so far as I can see, under the law, it is not necessary to include them in the public accounts.

I am informed that it is, that any expenditure of public money must

go into the public accounts, and surely expenditure on these lines will get into the public accounts.
I do not think the minister is any more sure about that than I am, and I am very suspicious about it.
I am informed by my deputy, who knows something about the routine, that these accounts must go into the public accounts.

Then why cannnot the minister bring down an estimate, just as has been done in the case of the other items? Let me give another example. There is in the Main Estimates, an item for principal and interest for maturing and matured loans, secured or unsecured. In other words, you provide in the Main Estimates for paying off principal, because that is what this amounts to. In this other case, we are incurring a principal charge. Why could that not be covered in the estimates, as well as the matter of paying off a principal charge? There is no difference in the principle of the thing. That is the point I want to make. This has already been suggested and turned down; but I would still suggest that this bill should pass as a general authority to do these works and then a special estimate, not necessarily included in the Main Estimates, but a special item in the Supplementary Estimates should be brought in for this year for, say $10,000,000. I wish the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) would listen to me, if he would be good enough, on this point. Every year that I have been in this House we pass ordinary Public Works estimates covering contracts which are already let for amounts away in excess of the amount voted. For instance, we let a contract for a million dollars for some public work. All we vote during the year is, perhaps, $500,000, knowing that during the year we shall require only that amount of money on the contract. The contract is let; the country is committed to the work; but the amount required for the year is estimated, and the amount inserted in the estimate. That is exactly what we are asking should be done in this case. Grant the authority to the railway company to go on with the capital expenditures, and then bring in a supplementary estimate covering the amount you want to spend this year. In my estimation, there is no difference in principle in providing the amounts in the Main Estimates in a proper and ordinary parliamentary fashion, and that called for in this bill in a special and extraordinary manner.

I do not want to delay my bill, but I have tried to point out the practicability of the matter. If my hon. friend has had any experience in public works, he will see one of the difficulties. This happens time and time again, and it should not happen with railway construction, particularly in the position in which the country is as regards labour. Construction should not be held up. What happens is that contractors are allowed to go on after an appropriation has run out; they finance themselves, and the cost of that public work is the cost plus the interest on the money which they advance. The counry in this way loses money. If the United States were to build the Welland Canal, 'they would pass a lump sum, and they would have to give an account each year. Until, however, the appropriation was exhausted, they would not have to come back to Congress for a further appropriation.

My hon. friend is not answering my argument at all. He is condemning the whole system of our estimates. I am not discussing that at all. That is the regular sysem, and I question the minister's expression of opinion as to its not being as good as that of the United States.

For large works, I am free to say that, I believe it is not. I have given my hon. friend one reason; I will give him another. Under the United States system, where a lump sum is voted, the work can go on without cessation and contractors can take advantage of every situation. With us, the work is sometimes halted for reasons pointed out by my hon. friend. With large works, our system is not the best for this reason: For a *work that will co^t, say $200,000, an amount of, perhaps, only $10,000 is voted. Unless some person reads Hansard with the explanation, he will believe that the work is going to cost only $10,000. Then, perhaps, he looks up Hansard the next year, and he finds there is $25,000 or $50,000 more. I believe the safe way in the public interest, is to put down at once the estimate for the entire amount, and to account each year to parliament. That is really what this is.
My hon. friend evidently thinks all these payments are to be shown in the public accounts. Do the payments made by the Canadian National Railways appear in the public accounts?

The amounts we advance them certainly do appear in the accounts.

Export Act-Pulpwood

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:	,
That it is expedient to amend section seven of the Export Act, chapter fifty of the Revised Statutes, 1906, as enacted by chapter thirty of the statutes of 1914, by providing that the Governor in Council may by regulation prohibit the exportation from Canada of pulpwood of the variety, kind, place of origin or having the particulars of identification or ownership or production described in the regulation.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I am a good deal in sympathy with the general principle of the resolution, but I should like my hon. friend to inform us whether he has made up his mind at all as to the regulations to be made respecting ownership and the like.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid the resolution can hardly be explained better than in its own words. It is to give the government power to make regulations having in view the prohibition of export of pulpwood. It might be a general prohibitory regulation without any qualification, or a regulation prohibiting export under certain conditions. For example, it has been suggested that it would he wise and expedient to exempt farmers who have pulpwood to clear off their land. We have not any plan in detail. If a plan is evolved we might put it in operation in a general way or subject to qualification; this would be a matter for further inquiry. The wording of the resolution implies that it may be desirable to distinguish respecting quality and character of wood.
I take it that this matter will receive the government's immediate attention and will not be tied up by the commission that was referred to at an earlier date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the terms of this resolution we would not be restricted, but much can be said in favour of having the report of a commission before acting.

I rose to express the hope that my hon. friend would really go on with the prohibition. I do not think he will gain any further information from a commission. The questions of ownership and so on would be just as real

if there is any real difficulty about them-after as before the report. I know my hon. friend is conversant with the whole matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure my hon.
friend that there are two sides to the question. Sometimes a commission has a good effect in educating the public in a matter which is not generally understood. I think there is more than one side to the question, and I do not wish to commit myself beyond that at the present stage.
Perhaps my hon. friend will go a little further and say that if there is to be a commission it will proceed with all speed and submit an early report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is desirable. More than that I could not say.

The prohibition of the export of pulpwood from farms owned by settlers would be very serious in the province of Quebec, especially in my own constituency. When new land is taken up by a settler he must clear it and dispose of the wood in some way or another. If his export to the United States is forbidden, he is at the mercy of the local dealer, if there is one, otherwise he has no market at all. The legislature of Quebec has refused to go that far; it prohibits the export of wood from Crown lands only. I presume the Dominion government will be guided very largely in this matter by the feeling in my province as expressed by the legislature. I certainly would view with alarm any action taken by this government to prevent the farmer or the settler from exporting his wood to the United States or anywhere else, because this is his only source of revenue until he has a crop to sell. Therefore I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will give us an assurance that these settlers will be exempt from any such prohibition.

Mr. Speaker, there is
not a county in all the Dominion where there are so many new settlers who have gone into the wilderness in the last ten years and established new homes as in my constituency. Along the National Railway about five hundred families have settled recently and cleared their holdings, and now they are looking to the American market to export their pulpwood. They are getting a better price across the line than they are getting on the Canadian side. These people expect that the law will remain as it is, and I hope that when the Minister of Finance gets the report of the commission that is to be appointed, he will take the requests of these people into consideration. I speak not only on behalf [DOT] of the new settlers, but on behalf also of farmers in my constituency who own land
Export Act-Pulpwood

and what might be called lots in second, third and fourth tiers and which are being retained for the purpose of cutting the wood thereon. They make a business out of it; they export these woods to the very best market. I know that many pulp mills in Canada own their own land, but they also buy from the farmers. I ask that these new settlers as well as the longer established farmers be protected by the minister in this respect.

I should think that the minister could look after both interests without trouble. The mill owners who are given certain rights in connection with these great national resources have some obligation to the state, I do'not know why the regulations should not go further than they do, and I do not know why the farmers and others should not be assured of a market for their pulpwood. After all, it is in the interests of the pulp people to preserve the forests; in many cases they have not much as it is. The pulpwood rates in the States are always low. The railway haul from Canadian points to American points is always expensive. It would be no very great hardship on the paper companies of this province if they had to buy the settlers' wood at a price which would equal the American price less the freights that the farmer would otherwise be out. The farmer would lose nothing and the country would be able to conserve its resources.

Is it the hon. gentleman's
suggestion that the government should fix a maximum price or a minimum price for the purchase of pulpwood?

No, there is
a market price; the matter of regulation would always be in the hands of the government. If they thought the farmers were being unfairly treated, they could act accordingly.

Who fixes the market
price?
The public demand in the States is fixing it every day.

It varies from county to
county.
It varies, but on what? Not on what affects the main price, but on the freight rates in that particular county and also on the man who is making the contracts in that particular county.

It varies with the man wh >
s making the contracts.

Of course the
government cannot look after all that, but there is a general scale in the market that is now being talked about, that is, the American market. It costs just so much to get into that market, and it should be no hardship to the Canadian manufacturer to take that pulpwood without the cost of the freight.
What is the real purpose of prohibiting the export of pulpwood?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is argued that the
forests are becoming destroyed, that we need to put on some general restrictions, and particularly that this is a Very valuable article that we need at home. There is much to be said on both sides of the question, but generally speaking the argument is that we should use it at home instead of exporting it. I am giving the current view on the subject; just how far we may act on this resolution is a question that remains to be con. sidered.
There are two sides to the question. One is that we are asked to prohibit the exportation of pulpwood in order to preserve our forests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Anything which diminishes the cut.

I notice that the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) holds the view that should an embargo be placed upon the export of pulpwood the opportunity of the sale of that wood would be lost to many of our farmers; and I suppose that applied more particularly to the county of Gaspq. The hon. member must disregard the market that is now available in Canada. I cannot quite see how he entertains the view that the placing of an embargo on the export of pulpwood would result in substantially the elimination of the market. I do not think that is the case.

If you bar out the American purchaser our farmers will be at the mercy of the Canadian paper makers, who will pay any price they like. Gaspe is far removed from Toronto and other places where they have mills, and our railway accommodation is very poor. The result of any such embargo as is proposed might cause those engaged in this industry to flock into the cities or go to the United States, as they are doing even now.

I must confess I do nut-share that outlook. First of all, if the embargo is put on there will still be the market as it exists to-day; there will be an increased market, as I believe. The paper mills will increase their output for sale in this country rather than for export and manufacture into paper across the line. The hon. member for Bonaventure says there will be a lack of competition and therefore a low price for the pulpwood. I think there are too many pulp mills in Canada to-day to admit of any fixed price. The putting on of an embargo will increase the number of our pulp factories; it will prevent the establishing of any set pri :e, and -will lead to competition as it does in any other industry. At the present time I presume that the hon. member for Bonaventure would not suggest that there is a combine among the pulp mills in Canada. Still less is it likely to be the case in the future wt-there will be an increase in the number of pulp factories.

I would draw the attention of the minister to the situation in our part of the country. In the county which I represent most of the land is Crown land. The farmers have wood on their land and almost
every year cut a certain number of cords of pulpwood which they offer for sale in the best market. For the last few years we have had to ship our pulpwood to the United States. In the latter part of last summer right in the little town where I live there were over two thousand cords shipped to the United States by water. These people are poor and have to work hard and I do not think we should deprive them of this chance to sell a few cords of pulpwood in the best market and if the market is not sufficient in our part of the country they should be allowed the chance to export to the United States. I would therefore ask the minister to reconsider the situation and not to do anything that will place at a disadvantage these poor people who have to work very hard for their living and who are making only a few dollars a year in this way. This measure is certain to cut their living, and I think that it should not be made applicable to pulpwood on Crown lands.

I want to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr, Marcil). The settlers in the constituency which I represent will certainly suffer if this measure goes into effect. There is probably a remark that should be made as to the different kinds of pulpwood that can be cut. It has been said by a previous speaker that the mills in Canada would buy all the pulpwood of our forests. For spruce and balsam there is a good local market I am told, but for poplar and basswood there is no market in this country or a veiy restricted market, and if this prohibition of export goes into effect the settlers will certainly suffer and not be in a position to sell all the pulpwood on their farms. Consequently I trust that the resolution will not be carried into effect.

I should like to say a
few words in support of the resolution because I believe that generally speaking it is worth trying. It is quite possible that the point made by my hon. friend from Saskatoon may have to be taken into consideration later, and that is one of the reasons why I believe the matter is better left in the hands of the Governor in Council, because if it was found that the farmer was really suffering because of this restriction on the export of pulpwood he should get consideration. I think that would be the desire of everybody. But we must not forget that the real market for pulp and paper is in the United States. Last year our exports of pulp, paper and forest products to the United States amounted to something like
Export Act-Pulpwood

$200,000,000, and the competition for pulp-wood will go on even though the export of pulpwood is discontinued. I made it my
business recently because my part of the country is very much interested' in this matter-we have many pulp and paper mills there, and the farmers are cutting and selling pulpwood from their land just as they are in the county of Bonaventure and other sections of the country that have been spoken of-I made it my business to make certain inquiries among those in a position to know and the general opinion was that if the export of pulpwood is prohibited the price will not decrease, because the internal competition among the mills is sufficient to keep prices to about the same level as at present. Yet if it were found that that was not the case and that the farmers were being injured by the fact that export was prohibited it would be a wise precaution on the part of the government to protect the farmer to that extent. But I am influenced more by the articles of Mr. Frank Barnjum. I have had the privilege of reading many of his articles for a long period now, and he knows the pulp and paper business I believe from the bottom up. I believe that he is absolutely sincere in making a stand at his own expense in the interests of the forests of this country. He has not only told us in his writings but. I have had the pleasure of having him tell me personally on a number of occasions that one of the greatest cures for the depletion of our forests is this very action that the minister proposes to take. I did not know that the minister was going to bring in this resolution. I had not seen any notice to that effect, and I had intended putting a resolution on the order paper next year along similar lines myself for the good of the country. I repeat, if we find that the farmers are suffering because of an order of this kind I believe that the prohibition of export should be taken off, but in the meantime I think that the minister is bringing forward legislation which should be supported by this House and be given a fair trial.

I rise to oppose this resolution. I may say at the outset that I am somewhat interested in that should the resolution pass my somewhat attenuated pocket-book will be still further attenuated. I may say also in order to be perfectly frank with the House that- if they consider that my judgment is not altogether disinterested they may at any rate give me credit for some knowledge of the question that is being discussed.

In the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario at the present time the exportation of pulpwood from Crown lands is prohibited. This' measure will have for effect the prohibition of the exportation of pulpwood cut from off private lands, that is, 11 p.m. lands held in fee simple, lands the entire property of which is vested in the owner. As the House is aware under the laws of Ontario, and I think notably in the province of Quebec certain very large tracts of timber lands are held under what is called license. The license amounts to a lease for which a yearly rental is paid, and this lease is practicallj'- everlasting provided the lessee fulfils his obligations and pays his rent. But what this measure aims at is to take control of the timber belonging to the owner of the land. It is just as if the government were to say to some of my Progressive friends from the West: Every bushel of wheat which you grow on your farms must be sold in Canada to the Canadian millers. I ask the government to tell us why there should be a discrimination between the farmer and the holder of timber lands. Take a farmer on one lot and alongside of him a man who owns a timber lot. The farmer may export to the four corners of the globe. The owner of the timber may only sell to five, six, ten or fifteen paper companies, most of whom have timber limits1 extending over an area of many miles and if the price does not suit them they can cut their own timber. Should this legislation go into force I foresee that the price of pulpwood in Quebec, at any rate, and I should imagine in Ontario, will hardl}1 pay for the cost of taking it out of the bush. It has been said I think that arrangements are to be made to exempt the farmer from this prohibition. How these regulations are to be made has not been explained to me, nor do I quite conceive of any means to be taken by the government to make such regulations. For instance, they say that a man who owns 100 acres of timber land is a farmer, and the man who owns 1,000 acres is not a farmer.
We have in Quebec seigneurial lands, some of them held since the early days of the French colonies, granted by the Kings of France. In 1S54, it is true, a great many of the feudal rights of these seigneurs were taken away, but even at that time compensation was given, and it was not thought proper to destroy the rights of ownership in the holdings of the seigneurs. These lands are held in some cases by the same family; in other cases they have been transferred from one to another for two or three centuries, and they will be affected by this regulation. In some

Export Act-Pulpwood
cases these seigneurs are farming their own lands, but they may have so many acres of timber lands held in fee simple. They may be farmers. Are the government going to say that because a man has more than 200 acres he shall not be treated as a farmer? Are they going to take away from these men rights which have been held for generations? To give an example of the manner in which some of these seigneurs have carried on their business, I quote the Seigneur of Lotbiniere, in the county of my hon. friend from Lotbiniere. The De Lotbiniere family have been there for a number of generations. The late governor, I think, of British Columbia, Sir Henry Joly de Lotbiniere, took a great interest in reforestation and forestry questions. He set to [DOT] work many years ago, and planted trees all over the estate, brought experts over from Germany and other countries in Europe; so that to-day he has a very fine estate, and the land is worth a great deal of money. Is it fair or just for this government t.o simply, by a stroke of the pen, say to the present owner of this estate, "You may not export this timber" and thus diminish the value of the seigneury by about one-fourth? I submit it practically means confiscation. It is neither fair, just nor right.
It has been said we are taking this step to preserve our forests, yet, if I understand the meaning of the minister aright, we are to allow the settlers to continue to ship the pulpwood which they cut to the United States but we are to prevent the seigneurs and other freeholders from doing so. Without having the figures before me I will venture to suggest to the government that at least 60 per cent of the pulpwood which is now being exported to the United States is being exported from the settlers' land. In a great majority of cases large companies or other people who own freehold lands have been very careful about getting rid of them because they have a considerable value owing to the very fact that pulpwood can be exported and with very few exceptions they have been carrying on reforestation and endeavouring, as it were, to farm their holdings. In view of the fact that within the last two or three weeks the eastern provinces have been devastated by vast conflagrations, and in view of the fact that the timber which was affected thereby must be cut next winter, otherwise it will have to rot in the bush, we will find in the spring of 1924 large quantities of pulpwood on the market. If I would be allowed to make a suggestion to the provincial governments of Quebec, Ontario, and New Brunswick, I would say that, instead of prohibiting the exportation, they should permit the exportation of pulpwood to the United States, at least for two or three years, in order to stabilize the pulpwood market; so that this timber which has been destroyed, or partially so, by fire and which will be eventually destroyed unless it is cut within one year may be exported to the United States and that the price will be, at least, sufficient to cover the cost of cutting down and taking it to the railways.
There is another phase of the situation. We have in this House, and particularly on this side of the House, been talking about and arguing at great length for freer trade, and for doing away with the barriers of trade, asking that we be given a chance to go into the American market. Here we are putting up, not a tariff but a Chinese wall, which prevents us selling to the American market. I submit wo are inconsistent, and that we are not carrying out our programme, our platform and our promises. Should such legislation be passed, we will be denying the very principles on which we are supposed to stand and we will be going back on everything the Liberal party holds sacred.
There is another phase of the situation. During the war and shortly afterwards I remember the chamber in the Victoria Museum building ringing with vehement utterances in which we decried government by order in council. Is there any more striking example of government by order in council than this resolution which is being brought down?
Hear, hear.

We have a blanket resolution which tells us nothing, and simply says that regulations will be made regarding pulpwood. I have every confidence in the government but I am sorry to say it must have been badly advised when it brought down this resolution. I have no doubt the time has come when a commission should be appointed to study the question. I have no objection to a commission, I think it would be a good thing. The people of this country have much to learn with regard to pulpwood and its exportation. Let us appoint a commission and let them make a full study of the question.
Does the hon. member know of any potential commissioners who are still at large?

No, but if the hon. member will give me the names of any I may recommend them. If the government announces its intention of naming a commission, there will be no difficulty in finding the com-
Export Act-Pulpwood

missioners. Let the government make a full and complete study of the question and if, after a study of the question, the commission brings in a report that the exportation of pulpwood shall be prohibited, I think the majority of the people will be willing to back up that statement, but until such time as the government has fuller information than it has, and until such time as this House has full information, I submit we should not enter hastily into any such legislation as that now before us.

This subject requires I think and will obtain the most careful consideration of this committee. I want to say something from the standpoint of the province of New Brunswick. I do not pretend to know the whole lumber or pulpwood situation in New Brunswick; but I can say to members of the House that, as in Quebec, there are the government lands which have unfortunately been most disastrously ravaged, first by the bud worm and in the last two weeks by fire. Our resources in that respect are considerably affected, and the government of that province must be seriously concerned with the question of what policy it shall adopt. We have also privately owned lands. For some reason the policy of New Brunswick has been to prohibit the export of pulpwood cut from government limits; but that prohibition has not been and, perhaps, could not be applied to privately owned lands, on all production of privately owned lands where there is not enough to support one pulp mill, because to impose a prohibition of exportation in absolute terms, would be really to throw people into the hands of local buyers. The government of New Brunswick has not compelled that course to be taken. Where an owner of freehold lands has also been a leaseholder from the province, the government has permitted him to export from Crown lands a quantity equal to that which he might have taken off his privately-owned lands, but so that t-he total quantity would not be greater than that which he sent out of the province. It was necessary to pursue a course of that kind. The policy I speak of is the one which was first adopted by New Brunswick. Then a succeeding government prohibited the exportation absolutely, and they had to come back to the original proposition because of the extreme difficulty of adjusting the pulpwood business.
Under these circumstances, I think legislation by order in council or directly requires the very closest co-operation and concurrence of the provincial governments. This, I think I may say, is a matter of vital importance to 
__
the government of New Brunswick as regards revenue. I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will say to me that his government will take all these things into consider-atiton. But may I ask: When will they do this? Between now possibly and the next session of parliament. But is it to be expected that any regulations in the nature of absolute prohibition would be brought into effect so quickly as that? Would not a period of time be given to allow the very serious readjustment which must take place of people's business? I would say that an anticipatory note of at least a year would only be fair, and yet I want to see every bit of forest value preserved for the people of this country. So far as the legislation is in that direction, it has my sympathy and it should have my support; but I want it to be brought into operation in such a way as to cause just as little dislocation of industry as possible. Therefore, I think I am right in assuming, and I think the minister will be one of the first in the House to concede that a change of the character ought not to be brought into effect instantaneously or with a notice of only two or three months. If that is conceded, I accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), which I think has great merit, that there should be a commission. I understand the minister is favourable to that. As regards naming commissioners, I do not think that there will be the slightest difficulty in obtaining them without resort to the ranks of party supporters on any of the three sides of this triangular House. One name, that of Mr. Frank Barnjum, stands out pre-eminently. He is a man who has spent a great deal of his money and who has devoted his energy to the work of endeavouring to preserve to the people of Canada that heritage which they possess in standing timber. A man of that character with another similar to him, associated with him, could give a report that would be of value, and it would come in quite time enough if we had it at the next session of parliament. I am not going to inveigh any more strongly than my hon. friend (Mr. Power) has just donq, against government by order in council. It is sufficient that the emergency of war has passed, and I think all parties agree that there should be as little government by order in council as there may be. Very much of the administration of the government of the country must be conducted by order in council; but when we come to a matter of such great importance as this, to a complete change of policy, I do not thint-it would be out of the way to ask that a

Export Act-Pulpwood
definite measure should be laid before and receive the sanction of parliament. Reading this resolution, how do I know, how does any other hon. member know whether this is a move-and it might be a right and proper move-on the part of the Minister of Finance in the direction of bargaining with the United States? It may be simply intended to force them to better terms with regard to their tariff. I would not reprobate it if it were for that purpose. Perhaps the minister cannot state that very publicly, and I would possibly vote for it if that element were in it. On the other hand, how do I know that with the comparatively limited view of the subject that must be taken in government circles, immense injury might not be done, not only to private interests, but to public interests in the provinces which would be principally affected? Therefore I say, before anything is done, there ought to be first a proper investigation. If that investigation is made by competent men and if the recommendation seems at all suitable to the conditions which they find, those recommendations ought, if possible, to be accepted by this House. But even before that, there ought to be an opportunity for discussion, for proper representation, for consideration, before we enter upon this thing which, however praiseworthy it may be in itself, may very easily lead to an absolute dislocation of a very important branch of industry, may stop employment, may drive people to the wall, and may seriously impair in the province from which I come the very funds upon which the government must rely in order to carry on the everyday business of that province. Therefore I join the hon. member for Quebec South in pressing, so far as I may do so, upon the minister the advisability of proceeding now by commission and letting the result of that commission come before the next session of parliament. Then let us have a government policy which will be clear and distinct, which we can debate here and to which, if we see any objection, we can suggest amendments, and perhaps suggest to the government some better course which will do good to all and harm to none.

I must congratulate the
government on the resolution now before the committee dealing with the question of an embargo on pulpwood.
In the recent budget debate, I spoke at some length on the subject of forest conservation; but I wish again to urge on hon. members of this House the great necessity of immediate and drastic steps being taken to conserve our forest wealth, and as a means to this end, to support this resolution which
empowers the government to take prompt action.
No element of consideration for what is considered individual rights of the estimated two per cent of Canadian farmers who wish to export pulpwood from Canada should be allowed to blur our vision or influence the hon. members of this House on whom rests the grave responsibility of safeguarding our national interests. This is not a matter of the moment; it is not a matter of respecting minority rights; it is a matter which makes for the weal or woe of Canada in the future. And in the light of clarified vision which will surely come in the future on this question, the parliament of 1923 will either in the future appear as the protector and preserver of Canada's great forest wealth or it will be blackened by its failure to act decisively and promptly in what must be considered a serious situation. We have often heard the argument advanced that the restriction of pulpwood export is a violation of individual rights and liberties.. In answer to this argument let me say that all laws for the benefit of a country as a whole must infringe on personal liberty. Where would this or any other country be if individual liberty of action were not controlled by laws when that action was detrimental to the general good? As well might one say that we should not control the personal liberty of our fishermen by establishing fishing seasons, or of our huntsmen by defining hunting seasons, as well as to say that we should allow pulpwood to be cut from fee lands at the owner's will regardless of the loss to the country as a whole. All are natural resources and as such can never be wholly individually controlled. An embargo on the exporting of pulpwood cut on fee land might apparently work hardships on a small percentage of the estimated farmers who wish to export it but ultimately it would result in public good by forcing pulp and paper companies to locate in Canada, thus increasing the home market for their products, both forest and agricultural and increasing the chances of employment for their children, capitalized industries sharing the weight of taxation under which Canadians labour to-day and will labour for some time to come.
Other countries, notably Norway, Sweden and Finland, the very countries which our Canadians meet as competitors for the world's trade in pulp and paper products have not hesitated to prohibit the export of pulpwood, and these great industrial countries are looking upon Canada with amazement that for a few petty obstacles she is acting the spendthrift with her forest wealth
Export Act-Pulpwood

The United States' capitalists whose business acumen is undoubted will accept this embargo as an evidence of ordinary business sense and already they are preparing for it by buying large tracts of available pulp lands; and the}' will locate plants here for the manufacture of raw material unless they are still allowed to get it out of the country to be manufactured into the finished article by their own workmen. It is estimated that the United States have only enough timber of their own to supply their mills for five or at most ten years. Are our Canadian forests to be depleted as under present conditions they surely will be by the United States while that country's supply is conserved? These are facts. Let me recite some of them. The original virgin forests of the United States amounted to 830,000,000 acres; at the present	time they have only
130.000.	000 acres. Their annual deforested	areas from	all causes total	26,-
000,000 acres. The United States depends on Canada for 50 per cent of its newsprint and 30 per cent of its pulp. Canada exports yearly of pulpwood 5,000,000 cords. Forest fires in Canada last year totalled 5,000 while the ravages of the bud worm destroyed 150,000,000 cords. The capital invested in Canada in pulp and paper industries approximates
8380.000.	000, with a yearly productive value of $200,000,000, providing employment for 30,000 people, with wages amounting to $28,000,000. The industry uses 644,805 horsepower or nearly one-third of the developed hydraulic resources of Canada. It is estimated that some of our large pulp and paper plants in Canada have barely five years' supply of wood in sight. In 1920, of Canada's cut of pulpwood, 31 per cent was exported to the value of $16,000,000. If exported as manufactured pulp instead of raw wood, the value would have been $84,000,000 and exported as paper, it would have been $105,000,000. If the collected data of indisputable facts can not convince us of the seriousness of the situation we must admit that as in olden times the Heavens have displayed signs of warning. The dense pall of smoke that has hung over Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific during the past few weeks, pervading even this building, is indubitable evidence of the wiping o it of our forests, and their approaching extermination if every possible method is not applied, and quickly applied, to stem this devastation. We must recognize these facts. Our commercial and agricultural prosperity will largely vanish with our forests; our hydraulic powers will be diminished; our fanning country will be left bare and arid; our

pulp and paper industries forced out of existence by lack of raw material, while Canadian money invested in these industries will be lost.. More than that, the exodus of our population in search of employment will b' greater. Our game and fur-bearing animals, a source of great wealth to Canada, will be homeless and will disappear, and Canada, the-land of primeval forests with their priceless value will be a tragic monument to the blunders of its legislators. This is not a party problem and we should not so consider it. It is far above the realm of partv. It reaches down to the very foundation of Canada's national existence, and the way in which we solve it means our continuance as a prosperous people or our speedy retrogression into national bankruptcy. It has been truly said that a dying forest means a dying nation. Let me urge hon. members of all parties in this House to disregard any local situation that may influence their action and support this resolution which authorizes immediate and effective action for the preservation of our forests.

I am fully in sympathy with the resolution. If the people of Canada do not look after their own interests and protect their forests, who will? Last fall I was up in the Cariboo country and I saw a lot of men working in the timber. I went over and found about two hundred Japs cutting our forest down. They were towing the logs down to Vancouver and putting them aboard Japanese ships for Japan. What was Canada receiving from her forests? Absolutely nothing.
Was this in the form of logs?
I said logs.
This resolution covers pulpwood only.

Well, what is pulpwood but logs cut into small portions? I have seen in British Columbia the finest logs ever taken out for pulpwood. You do not grow the class of timber down here that we grow in British Columbia. Some years ago I noticed that on every dollar's worth of manufactured goods shipped out of the United States 85 per cent represented labour, while for every dollar's worth shipped out of Canada only 10 per cent represented labour. It is about time that we manufactured our natural resources and got the utmost out of them. If this pulpwood exportation is stopped it will only be a few years before the American concerns will be establishing factories on the Canadian side

Export Act-Pulpwood
of the line and giving employment to our people; and that is what we want.

I endorse the remarks of
the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride).
I think it is time we also drew the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to the exportation of raw material from British Columbia in the form of logs. Ruthless destruction of our forests is proceeding and in another generation the forests of Vancouver island will pretty well have disappeared. I have seen one of the grandest forest areas of America wiped out in one generation,-the forest area of the state of Michigan is now a farming country. We do not want our potentialities to be wasted without getting some proper return. I do not think we fully realize what we lose by the exportation of pulpwood. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken quoted some figures. I have other figures which I think will prove conclusively that it is time we did something.
In 1920, 31 per cent of our pulpwood was exported for which we received in round numbers, $16,000,000. We exported 28 per cent as pulp with a value of $76,000,000; 25 per cent as paper worth $87,000,000. Had the $16,000,000 worth of pulpwood exported-been converted into pulp, it would have had a value of $84,000,000; if into paper, $105,000,000,- making a loss to labour, to capital and to Canada of from $68,000,000 to $89,000,000 in one year.
Surely, Sir, this exportation of raw material is the acme of economic folly. In 1921 we produced 2,180,578 cords of pulpwood which were converted into pulp and paper worth $108,677,520. We exported 1,902,533 cords of pulpwood to the United States for which we received only $14,617,610. "And so the play goes on." The folly of it must be apparent to all honourable members.
In Canada we have invested in pulp and paper plants $380,000,000 and an army of men are employed. Why not keep all raw material at home and with it another capable army of men that is leaving for the United States following our raw products to engage in their manufacture. They are following our raw products just as they are following our $172,000,000 which constitute our adverse trade balance with our American neighbours. We are being bled white by our neighbours. Certainly no company would conduct business along these lines, and no country can persist in doing so and not precipitate national disaster. The cry of the world is for lumber and paper. Let us take full advantage of our splendid opportunities and aim for maximum results. Despite
substitutes, the demand for lumber is continually increasing. Yet, Sir, we of British Columbia sit idly by while immense booms of our saw logs are being towed across the line to the state of Washington and our men are following to work in the mills of that state.
It is time we awoke to the necessity of doing something. It is said that if we prohibit the export of pulpwood the Americans might retaliate by placing an embargo on anthracite.
I think if we got our house in order this is the best thing that could happen. In Alberta vve have immense areas of coal which even at present prices would make it good policy for Ontario to buy in preference to looking to Pennsylvania for her fuel requirements. In British Columbia we also have immense coal areas, but it is out of the question to ship our coal so far east as Ontario. In Nova Scotia there are also immense supplies of coal available which could be placed on the market in Ontario at a price just as cheap as that charged for American coal. Why not bum Canadian coal and so s-ave the many millions of dollars that we pay the Americans every year?
We send our pulpwood over to the American side and our men follow to engage in the work of manufacturing it into paper, which is worth many times more than the raw material. We are simply throwing ourselves into the arms of those people who say, "We do not want a pound of your butter unless you pay an import tax of eight cents a pound." At the same time we allow their butter to come into Canada on payment of a duty of only four cents a pound. Why turn our cheek to these people? For every cord of pulpwood that goes over there we may say that six dollars is lost in labour for every dollar that comes into this- country. When we consider that we are losing from $70,000,000 to $90,000,000 by the exportation of pulpwood, is it not time that we quit temporizing and took a bold stand even if somebody has to suffer? And somebody must suffer, but we can easily recompense the five hundred farmers or so who may be hurt by the prohibition of the export of pulpwood. I would impress on the minister the urgent necessity of looking into the exportation of saw-logs from British Columbia. There, by adroit legislation, we have what amounts to an export tax on all timber cut in the country on privately-owned land, but if the wood is worked up in sawmills the tax is remitted. I think the tax runs to about $1.50 per thousand, but that is not sufficient to repay the national loss. We have many American companies operating in British Columbia, and I know one institution that

has spent over a million dollars on a logging railroad. Every log from that camp is sent across to the American side and our men are following the logs to work in the American mills.
How can we expect to succeed unless we take a bold step? Let us use our own coal and manufacture our own forest wealth, and see if we cannot set an example to the world of a country that does not have to tell its people: We cannot pay our way year by year.

In my part of the country
the people cut most of their wood in the month of June, and therefore if this prohibition of export went into effect at once it would mean a great loss to them. As they are dependent on the returns from their wood to pay their taxes and expenses, I trust the government will defer putting this proposed legislation into effect for this season, so that the people I have referred to may have sufficient time to become acquainted with the regulations and act in accordance therewith.

I am entirely in accord with any effective steps that may be taken to preserve our timber supply,and I think something along the lines of this resolution is necessary as one of those effective steps. But I do not think it will get us very far alone, it must be part of a much more comprehensive policy. In the matter of principle I associate myself very earnestly with the views expressed by my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie). Indeed, I believe that the law and the prophets is pretty much in his words. I am of course compelled to* admit that his sentiments, while good horse business sense for this Dominion, are sadly out of harmony with those idealistic principles of free trade which we once heard so frequently from hon. gentlemen opposite, but which wa now hear no more. I had some sympathy with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when he displayed an abhorrence of broken pledges and principles and showed that in its every feature this was a violation of those things for which his party was professing, and had in the past very emphatically professed, to stand, and which it yet proclaims as some beautiful ideal that it loves but is sorry that it cannot reach much sooner; all the while it is moving directly the other way. I know they have to fly in the face of every profession to pass this legislation. There is only this to be said: They must always do this if we are ever to get any sensible legislation. We must either do without the government or do without the sensible legislation. But 
my objection to this resolution is mainly another urged by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). It is not legislation at all. It does not even foreshadow legislation; it is simply a proclamation of the government to the House of inability to frame legislation. They say: We cannot bring any legislation before you; we cannot work it out; we have not any policy, but if you will give us the summer we will try to frame something, and we want authority now from the House to make it legislation. In other words, they say: We who almost destroyed our vocal organs for years denouncing order in council government come here and ask for power to pass any orders on earth respecting this new form of policy. Nor is this bill different from any other bill. The hon. member for Quebec South thought this perhaps the most audacious yet offered to get order in council powers, but it is not a particle worse than the last bill. In the worst days of the war- and war times are very different from peace times-powers of this kind were not asked for save on matters directly concerning the prosecution of the war.
What about the Grand Trunk?
As to the Grand Trunk, we came down with all the conditions, all the principles affecting the legislation.
By order in council.
No, in the bill. Look at the act. Look at the Canadian National Railway Act; look at the Grand Trunk Acquirement Act.
Was not the acquisition accomplished by order in council?

No, not at all. Why, the Grand Trunk Pacific was laid at our door, pitched at us by the management. They wrote us a letter on the third of May and told us that on the tenth of May they would be out of business.
The right hon. gentleman is right.

Certainly I am right. In acquiring the Grand Trunk we asked parliament for all the powers and stated the terms upon which the road would be acquired. Had we proceeded as I will describe in a moment, we would have followed the course adopted here now. Had we brought in a resolution which read as follows: The Governor in Council may acquire the Grand Trunk railway upon such terms and conditions and at such price as may be fixed and according to such regula-

Board of Audit
tions as may be passed by the Governor in Council,-that is the resolution we would have introduced had we followed the course this government is following in introducing this resolution; nor would it have been a bit more audacious. Look at the Grand Trunk Acquirement Act and compare it with this. There is nothing left to regulation except the merest detail. The whole principle of acquirement, the terms of acquirement-everything is there. That is what the government ought to have here. That is legislation; this is not legislation at all. It is merely a flouting of parliament, by those who -were supposed to be rescuing the country from the evils of order in council government, by those who were going to bring back the days of control by legislation. What control is parliament going to have here? The government may do something or it may not. If it does anything, it may do it on whatever terms it likes. It may exempt whomever it likes; it may bring within the circle of the legislation whomever it likes. It may bring one province in and let another province out; there is nothing it may not do if legislation following this resolution passes. Again I say this is not foreshadowing legislation; it is merely asking for a blank cheque from the House of Commons that the government may pass what legislation it may deem wise or expedient for itself later on. It is to be expected that those who talk the loudest about the return to control by parliament are those who act the most defiantly in the very face of parliament when they are in power. I protest against that feature of the resolution and I ask the government to come down with a bill stating upon what terms they propose to prevent the exportation of pulpwood. If the terms are reasonable, I will support them. I am in favour of the principle. I know there are some who will be injured by it, but the individual interest, subject perhaps to proper compensation, must needs bow to the general good. I say I am in favour of the principle, but I ask for legislation. I do not like being asked day after day, sometimes half-a-dozen times a day, simply to sign a parliamentary cheque to an administration which hopes at some later time to be able actually to evolve a bill.

Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 84, an Act to amend The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mr. MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved:
speechtext:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this House disagrees to their amendments to Bill No. 84, an act to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907, for reasons that the said amendments defeat the objects aimed at in the bill and would complicate rather than simplify procedure.
He said: This bill as originally introduced into the House of Commons had as its object the amendment of sections 15, 27 and 58. No new features were proposed, the amendments seeking simply to convey more clearly the intent of those sections as they had been generally understood; also in the case of section 58 a specific penalty was provided for an offence with regard to which in the statute as it had stood a penalty was implied but not stated. The principal amendment was that whereby in section 57 it is provided that where employer or workmen intend or desire to make a change in wages or hours "it shall be unlawful for the employer to make effective a proposed change in wages or hours or for the employees to go on strike until the dispute has been finally dealt with by a board and a copy of its report has been delivered through the registrar to both the parties affected." This proposed amendment in no way varies the intent of the clause but makes its meaning indisputable. In the amending bill this same section 57 is further amended by requiring that "the application for the appointment of a board shall be made by the employers or employees proposing the change in wages or hours." Whilst it has seemed clearly the intent of the statute that an application for the establishment of a board should proceed from the party proposing any such change as contemplated, yet this is not expressly stated, and, in the case of the several hundred boards which have been established in the past sixteen or seventeen years, the applications from the employers have been few in number, not, in fact, exceeding more than two or three per cent, a situation which has worked serious in-
Industrial Disputes

justice to the workmen and has naturally aroused their resentment. Under the amendment proposed by the Minister of Labour when the employer proposed a change it would be his duty to make application for a conciliation board.
The amending bill passed the House of Commons without change. As the bill has been returned to this House, its object with respect to clarification of section 57 is entirely defeated, whilst an additional clause affecting the appointment of the chairman of a board has been added to the bill, which, if accepted, would tend seriously to delay and embarrass those administering the statute. The bill as it is now before parliament leaves section 57 without the clarifying additions proposed in the amending statute, but with a clause added which is quite inconsistent with and contrary in its effect _to the main clause, for whereas clause 57 as it now stands provides quite clearly that a change with regard to wages and hours cannot be made effective until any dispute arising has been "dealt with by a board and a copy of its report has been delivered through the registrar to both the parties affected;" yet the proposed amendment of the upper House apparently seeks to have the proposed change effective as soon as the application for a board has been made.
The effect of this portion of the proposed addition to section 57 is therefore to render the whole section contradictory and confusing as between its different paragraphs. The remainder of the clause proposed as supplementary to section 57 adds to the confusion . by introducing a reference to the retroactive character of the findings of a board. The reference in question does not actually add to the authority which a conciliation board has always been free to exercise, and, with regard to the declaration contained in the last sentence of the supplementary clause that "on the failure of either party to abide by the decision of the board, the other party may have recourse to a strike or lockout as the case may be," this also in no way increases or extends the rights or powers of the parties to a dispute beyond those which they would in any case possess under the statute. The amendment of the upper House with respect to section 57 would, therefore, have the effect of confusing, complicating and delaying procedure, without bringing compensating benefit of any kind.
The amendment proposed by the upper House with regard to section 8 respecting the appointment of a chairman introduces a new feature. The statute as it stands provides for
(Mr. Murdock.]
the selection of a chairman by joint agreement when possible of the other two members of a conciliation board, and requires that, where no agreement is reached, the minister shall make the necessary appointment. In about one-half of several hundred boards which have been established a chairman has been secured by agreement. It had become a general though not invariable practice for the Minister of Labour, when called upon to appoint a chairman, to select a judge, but this practice ceased when two or three years ago the Judges' Act was so amended as to prohibit the acceptance by a judge of the fees ordinarily payable to a chairman or member of a conciliation board. It is true that the Minister of Labour is not under the Judges' Act, as it has been amended, prohibited from asking a judge to act as a chairman, nor is a judge apparently prohibited from accepting a chairmanship; but since fees are no longer payable in such circumstances to a judge, it has not been thought reasonable as a rule to request a judge to undertake the duties involved in a chairmanship; such duties, it will be understood, are frequently of a severe and arduous nature and in nearly all cases are of the highest moment to employers and to large numbers of workmen, as well as frequently to the public. In two cases since the amendment of the Judges' Act, judges have been, however, appointed, once by the Minister of Labour of the late administration and once by the present Minister of Labour, but in the latter case the appointment was made on the joint recommendation of the other board members. In both cases the judges concerned accepted from a sense of public duty; no fees were of course paid them. It may be said that there is every advantage in a chairman being secured by joint agreement and the Minister of Labour appoints a chairman with reluctance. Inquiry shows that this has been the case with most previous ministers. The chances of an agreement are manifestly increased when a chairman is secured by joint request of other board members. The method or system, however, under which different Ministers of Labour have made appointments has not been the subject of any known criticism, and certainly the files contain no communications requesting or suggesting a change in the present practice. The objections to the system laid down in the Senate amendment are obvious. In the first place, the appointment of a chairman by a chief justice, whether the Chief Justice of a province or of the Supreme Court of Canada, would entail inevitable delay. Such delays would be particularly unfortunate since,

Industrial Disputes
despite every effort under present procedure, one side or other of the disputing parties is sometimes disposed to object to the time necessarily occupied in procedure. In the second place, a chief justice or other judge cannot possibly be as intimately seized of the nature of the dispute involved and of the particular type therefore of man wanted for the chairmanship as would be the Minister of Labour, who has established the board and has been in touch with details of procedure from its inception. It would be impossible to convey to a judge at a distant point by correspondence, which would of necessity be us a rule by telegraph with consequent expenditure and some danger of inaccuracy, all the particulars which should be properly at hand to enable the judge to reach a correit conclusion as to the type of person apparently best suited for the important duties involved. The judge would exericse his best judgment and the appointment might or might not prove to be a good one. In any case the minister who is charged with the administration of the statute would be freed from responsibility on this most vital aspect of administration and the judges would become involved in the technicalities of departmental procedure. Since a considerable proportion of the disputes dealt with under the statute extend tj two or more provinces, the task of naming the chairman of conciliation boards would under the proposed Senate amendment fall most frequently to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, who from the nature of his functions may be presumed to be furthest removed from contact with industrial disputes and necessarily therefore the more dependent on the advice of others as to the type of person best suited for a chairman. Despite the high legal and other attainments which a chief justice would undoubtedly possess, it is submitted that, in addition to the complication and delays in procedure which the proposed system of appointing chairmen would entail, the suggested change would be highly detrimental to the successful administration of the statute. I would, therefore, move that the amendments of the Senate be not concurred in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I was not in at the moment the minister started. Would he tell the committee what he was reading from?

A carefully prepared
statement indicating the views on the amendments that have been made to Bill No. 84 since it left this House.
Indicating whose views?
The reader's views.

I have no objection to that. I did not know the minister was reading his speech. I thought he was fortifying his position from some real authority. In fact, I rather commend the intiative the minister has shown to-night in being very careful to read his speech.
Does the right hon. gentleman not consider the Minister of Labour a real authority on labour matters?
There are certain things he is not a real authority on as I am compelled to admit reluctantly.
In the matter of labour legislation, the right hon. gentleman will admit that the Minister of Labour is a good authority.

As regards legislation he may be a very good workman, I have no doubt. If there is to be a difference between the Senate and the House of Commons in this matter I think I can offer a solution. In general I have no objection to the minister naming the third arbitrator in cases where it is essential that an outside party be named to act in that capacity. I think I may say it has been very general up to a certain time, as set out in the memorandum read by the minister and prepared by himself-* well, I do not know that I can say that it was prepared by himself-that the person appointed was a judge. But as the memorandum states, since the time when by statute of this parliament, the judges were forbidden to accept outside remuneration, there has been some difficulty apparently in having judges act in such cases. I want to say very frankly that I do not think there should be any difficulty in having judges act in these matters, and in my opinion the statute should be amended so as to provide that the taking on of work of this kind shall be obligatory on the judge. I believe that the judges of this country to-day receive ample remuneration for the work they do, particularly the county court judges, who formerly did act under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. There are county court judges in this province who have not enough work to keep them-I almost said warm-at the present time, and why they should not be willing to serve the country by officiating as arbitrators under the Industrial Disputes Act I do not know. At the time the bill was passed which

i

prevented their taking extra remuneration for commission work, the judges' salaries were very substantially raised, and if they decline to act in such an appropriate capacity as that of arbitrator under the Industrial Disputes Act then, I ask, why does not the government bring in a measure to make this work a part of the duties of county court judges, or, for that matter, of other judges?

speechtext:
Can we define their
duties?

courts is within provincial jurisdiction.

The constitution of the
courts is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, of course; but we can add to the duties of the judges. As a matter of fact we have done so. For example, we make the duties of judges obligatory under our Elections Act.

The constitution and
procedure of the courts comes within the jurisdiction of the	provinces. The only
matter that appertains to federal authority is the appointment of the judges. Does not my hon. friend think that it would be ultra vires for the federal authority to impose extra burdens on any judge?

The first proposition of
my hon. friend is right, that the constitution and the procedure of the court are matters of provincial jurisdiction. But as to what a judge shall do is not a matter of procedure nor does it relate to the constitution of the court. Under our Dominion Elections Act and under our Controverted Elections Act, for instance, we assigned duties to judges.
Within the province.
Yes, within the province. And we assign duties to the judges under the Criminal Code. In fact, there are statutes galore of this House assigning duties to judges.

My hon. friend is a
clever lawyer. We should like him to explain that point.
I thought I was explaining it. I say that in our Criminal Code we assign duties to the judges.

The Criminal Code
is federal in its constitution.
	,
Certainly, and so is this a matter of federal jurisdiction or we should not be passing it.
Does that assign duties to judges?

Yes. The regular judges are assigned duties under these various federal statutes, for the purposes designated, and this has been the practice for a great many years. It is immaterial whether or not they are assigned the duties in their function as judges; so long as they are assigned those duties it becomes obligatory on the judges to perform them; and why they should not perform these particular duties, which are pre-eminently of a judicial character, I cannot see. They are the proper persons to perform those duties. If the judges are made eligible I do not object to the minister being given the power to name the third arbitrator. I apprehend that what those who object to the bill in the form in which it passed this House have in mind is that the minister, not being able to appoint judges, will appoint some person whom he wishes to favour or who in his opinion will give a judgment suitable to himself. It is that fear that has no doubt animated the amendments, and we could remove it by making it compulsory on judges to accept this work. I cannot speak for the other House, of course, but it seems to me that it might well be agreed that if this work is made the compulsory duty of judges, the objections which the Senate entertained to the bill as it passed the House of Commons would be removed.

Does not my hon. friend think it would be advisable in the case of any dispute in a province to let the Governor in Council of the province name the arbitrator, seeing that they would be more familiar with the conditions?
I do not like the principle of this House passing legislation to enable another government to appoint anyone.
I was not suggesting that; I was merely asking my hon. friend for his opinion.

Well, my opinion is in the negative, and I will argue the matter more in detail when a bill of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) comes up. To my mind the right thing to do is to assign these duties to the judges. That done, it seems to me that the basic objection to the legislation would be removed.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING fPrime Minister): I gather from what my right hon. friend says that he assumes that the Senate had in mind in its recommendation that the minister might make a partisan appointment or appoint someone for personal reasons. I think my hon. friend is mistaken in any view that the minister has done anything of the kind, or that the records of the past will show any such thing. If one looks over the list of those appointed as chairmen of boards of arbitration, one will be struck with the circumstance that for the most part the chairmen have been remarkably free from partisan bias.
That would not apply to Alex. Smith.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Alex. Smith is an able lawyer and his part as arbitrator went to show that his selection was a remarkably good one. We can only judge of the worth of appointees by the nature of the service they render, and my hon. friend will find that the chairmen of practically all boards have really given remarkable satisfaction in the generality of cases so far as the discharge of their duties is concerned. It is not for us, I think, to assume what the motives were, but one realizes that in the other Chamber they are inclined to look to the courts for many matters to which we in this House would look to ministers responsible to the House and through the House to the public; end it would be a mistake to get away from that responsibility which ministers of the Crown have to parliament for appointments that are made. There is a large field to draw from apart from the courts. There are many business men of wide experience such, for example, as college professors, and men of the legal and other professions, and there is a very large body of public-spirited persons who take interest in social and economic questions. That whole field is open from which to select chairmen for boards of arbitration. I agree with my right hon. friend that the judges have in many cases made excellent, chairmen. In the case of county court judges I think it ought to be made possible to have them selected in any event as chairmen of boards of arbitration; but I certainly would be strongly opposed to giving to the chief justice of a province the naming of the third arbitrator. I think the appointment should remain where it is at present, in the hands of the minister.
