speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext: I heartily concur in the remarks made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), and submit that the amendments made by the Senate ought not to be accepted. The right hon. leader of the Opposition stated that in some provinces county court judges should act as third arbitrators.
I did not say in some provinces, I said everywhere.

In the province of Quebec we have no county court judge system; our judiciary are either judges of the superior court or of the circuit court. From my province frequent demands are made on the Department of Justich and the government for the appointment of new judges, our present judges not being able to cope with the work. But the question before the House is whether a judge of the Supreme Court-or as with us in the province of Quebec, a judge of the superior court'-should have the appointment of third arbitrator after one has been named by each of the contending parties. I submit that this has a tendency to drag the whole judicial system more or less into the political arena. When we have strife between employers and employees there is always a good deal of tension, and it seems to me that is just the time when the Minister of Labour, a responsible member of the government, should appoint the third arbitrator.
I look with certain misgivings upon the Senate interfering in labour matters to the extent they have done in this particular cas'e. The Senate, as we know, cannot deal with money matters, these being peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the Commons. Now, it seems to me that labour matters are something in which labour is particularly concerned, and consequently I think that an irresponsible body like the Senate ought to have enough wisdom to refrain from interfering.

Will the hon. member
tell us what the Senate should deal with?

Industrial Disputes
I submit that they ought to be a kind of rubber stamp to concur in the legislation sent up by the Commons in labour matters.
Order.

I am not speaking generally, but I think labour matters ought to be peculiarly for the Commons alone to deal with and not an irresponsible body like the Senate. The Minister of Labour in the past has been making these appointments, and there has been no complaint whatever. If any appointment does not meet with the approval of the people, the minister is responsible and, indirectly, the government of which he is a member. Surely that ought to be satisfactory to this House and to the Senate, and I must protest most vigorously against the Senate interfering in labour legislation affecting, as it does, the people.
We have under our constitution three divisions of government-the legislative, the judicial and the administrative. Now, our judges pass upon cases submitted to them, they address juries, they sift evidence, and they give their judgment in accordance with the facts. But when you have a judge mixed up in disputes1 between capital and labour, where the decision is bound to react upon the judiciary, I say-

My hon. friend as a
lawyer of many years' standing must know that the law is for the judge while the facts are always for the jury to find.

I think we can pass that
remark off with a laugh. It does not deserve anything better.
My hon. friend does not know the difference.

The hon. gentleman probably wished to sidetrack me, and to that extent I think he has succeeded. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am most vigorously opposed to the amendments to this legislation, and would suggest that they be sent back in order that that august body may have another opportunity of pondering the legislation and passing it in the form in which it was first sent up by this House.

I am not rising for the purpose of absolutely contradicting my friend, but I have every respect for the gentlemen who constitute the upper Chamber and deprecate their being reflected upon in any way. There was a time in my short life when I was wont to oppose the second Cham-

ber, but my experience as law clerk in the legislative council of Nova Scotia has led me to believe that an upper chamber is absolutely essential. It is the good old English system and I think it is good enough for Canada. All I ask in regard to this particular piece of legislation is this: I am thoroughly in accord with the principle that the judges should have the right to deal with all things that come before them, and if it is necessary to appoint a judge to act as arbitrator in a particular matter, the minister should have that right. The minister should retain the right to appoint an arbitrator where there is a difference of opinion between the employer and employee. The Senate has said that in such cases the tasks should be undertaken by the chief justice in the province concerned. In many cases the chief justice does not know the facts of the case. The minister has an opportunity of knowing all the circumstances. He gets the representations of the employees as well as of the employer, and he is in a position to name a man who should act. I believe that the judges should not have to deal with any controversial matter which may be of political significance. They are appointed to administer justice as between plaintiff and defendant in a civil matter and as between the King and his subjects in a criminal matter, and they should not be called upon to adjudicate in anything of a controversial character. I repeat that the upper chamber is what may be called a sober second thought in the matter of legislation and when they undertake to relieve the adjudicators of this land from dealing with matters which may be of a controversial political character, they are doing the right thing.

I do not wish to make any extended remarks on this amendment, but I desire to oppose it, not merely because the Senate has offered the amendment, lor because I think the judges are opposed to labour when they act as arbitrators in matters of labour disputes, but because I think the Labour department, as representing at least to some extent the voters of the country, is surely in a better position to act in this matter than the judges would be. The bill as drawn meets with the approval of organized labour; therefore I oppot'e the amendment made in this regard and hope the bill will be sent back to the Senate as originally drafted.

Mr. Speaker, just one
word.

The department would
be glad indeed if it were possible to utilize the services of judges as heretofore. I was rather surprised to hear my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition suggest that we might go back to that desirable system, because it was in 1921 when he led the government that provision was made under which it became impossible thereafter to utilize the services of judges in such cases1. We have found that judges are like other working men, like ordinary labourers-no pay, no overtime. In other words, with their regular duties and responsibilities before them and a specific salary for the performance of those duties, they are not willing-and I am not criticising them-to take on additional responsibilities without the additional compensation that is given to a private person who undertakes such extra work. But the amendments made by the upper House to section 57 are the most important, because their effect would be to make section 57 confused and complicated and to delay the procedure connected with the handling of boards of investigation, to say nothing of delay in getting results under the provisions of the act.
